4.5.3.3  Challenges for Energy Storage Deployment 
Interconnection Constraints 
The PJM interconnection process represents one of the most significant barriers to timely storage deployment. 
While recent reforms have improved efficiency, study times can still take up to two years and queue congestion 
results in slow processing that delays project deployment and can increase project costs. The withdrawal of projects 
in the queue can shift upgrade costs to remaining projects, creating uncertainty and cost risk. These factors 
complicate project planning, increase development risk, and can delay critical capacity additions needed for 
reliability. 
Local Governance and Siting Challenges 
Project siting is further complicated by variability in local zoning and permitting requirements, including setbacks, 
height limits, and screening requirements; noise restrictions; and fire safety standards and emergency response 
readiness. This variability limits site selection flexibility and requires extensive stakeholder engagement and 
education, particularly related to battery safety. Effective stakeholder engagement and transparent communication 
will be essential to maintaining project momentum and securing necessary approvals.

==== 2026-integrated-resource-plan-update.pdf — page 40 ====
39 
 
Supply Chain Constraints 
Despite declining technology costs, supply chain challenges remain a key risk, including long lead times for critical 
equipment (battery modules, power conversion systems, transformers); concentration of manufacturing in global 
markets, particularly Asia; and emerging domestic content and Foreign Entity of Concern requirements that affect 
procurement and tax credit eligibility. These constraints can impact project schedules and costs. 
Energy storage will play a critical role in enabling a reliable, affordable, and increasingly decarbonized grid. Li-ion 
technology provides a proven, scalable solution for near-term deployment, while LDES represents a potential 
solution to support higher renewable penetrations and long-duration reliability needs. 
The Company’s strategy of deploying near-term Li-ion capacity while piloting and evaluating emerging LDES 
technologies positions it to meet policy targets while managing risk and uncertainty. However, achieving long-term 
storage goals will require addressing systemic challenges related to technology and development cost, 
interconnection, supply chains, siting, and market design. 
 
4.5.4  Wind Resources 
 
4.5.4.1  Offshore Wind 
In August 2024, Dominion Energy secured the rights for a 176,505-acre lease area off the coast of Virginia Beach, 
adjacent and to the east of where the Company’s Coastal Virginia Offshore Wind (“CVOW”) Project is currently 
under construction (approximately 35 nautical miles from the mouth of the Chesapeake Bay). Winning the lease 
provides Dominion Energy with the option to pursue additional offshore wind development in the mid-Atlantic, and 
the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management indicates the lease area could support between 2.1 GW and 4.0 GW of 
offshore wind energy generation.  
The Company has also acquired a portion of an offshore wind lease for 38,964 acres off the coast of North Carolina, 
which will allow for development of an 800 MW offshore wind facility—enough to power 200,000 homes and 
businesses. 
4.5.4.2  Onshore Wind 
Consistent with the VCEA, the Company continues to evaluate onshore wind as a potential supply-side resource 
within a diverse portfolio of carbon-free generation resources. Onshore wind’s role is limited due to the 
Commonwealth’s relatively constrained wind resource potential (concentrated along a limited number of high-
elevation ridgelines in the western portion of the Commonwealth) and the challenges associated with siting, 
permitting, and developing new projects. Prospective sites are also generally located in remote areas that may 
require significant transmission upgrades or new interconnection facilities, increasing project costs and development 
timelines. 
Despite these challenges, the Commonwealth’s first utility-scale onshore wind project is nearing completion and 
represents an important milestone in Virginia’s renewable energy development. The project demonstrates that 
onshore wind can be successfully developed in Virginia under appropriate site-specific conditions and will provide 
valuable operational experience regarding resource performance, environmental management, and grid integration. 
The Company will continue to evaluate onshore wind resources as part of its “All of the Above” approach to 
resource planning.

4.5.5  Nuclear Resources 
For more than half a century, nuclear energy has provided reliable, around-the-clock, carbon-free electricity to meet 
customer demand. As the need for reliable, increasingly clean power grows, nuclear energy remains essential to 
maintaining both reliability and affordability. Dominion Energy has received approval to extend the operating lives of 
its existing nuclear units in Virginia; Surry Units 1 and 2 will now operate through 2052 and 2053, respectively, and 
North Anna Units 1 and 2 will operate through 2058 and 2060, respectively. The Company also continues to 
evaluate opportunities to expand its nuclear portfolio through advanced nuclear resources, including small modular 
reactors (“SMRs”).  
The Company continues to develop its North Anna Power Station site for the potential deployment of new nuclear 
and currently holds licenses and permits that could support the development and construction of one or more SMRs 
or a new large nuclear reactor. At the federal level, the Company holds an Early Site Permit (“ESP”) and a 
Combined Construction Permit and Operating License (“COL”). The ESP from the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory 
Commission (“NRC”) approves the site for a future nuclear power facility and considers site-specific safety and 
environmental matters. The ESP is also applicable to potential future SMR development. In July 2026, the Company 
filed an application with the NRC to renew the ESP for an additional 20-year term. The existing permit expires on 
November 27, 2027. Maintaining the ESP supports long-term planning flexibility by preserving the option to deploy 
future nuclear generation technologies at the North Anna site, subject to future regulatory approvals and resource 
planning determinations. The COL currently held by the Company is to construct and operate a GE-Vernova Hitachi 
Nuclear Energy Economic Simplified Boiling Water Reactor (“ESBWR”). Should the Company utilize its existing 
COL for licensing and deployment of a reactor technology other than the GE Hitachi ESBWR, it would necessitate a 
COL amendment. 
In addition to the federal licenses, the Company currently holds an Operational Water Withdrawal permit from the 
Virginia Department of Environmental Quality (“VDEQ”) for the operational requirements associated with the 
ESBWR. 
Federal policy support for new nuclear has increased, and interest in nuclear as firm, carbon-free power has grown, 
particularly from large-load and industrial customers. At the same time, new nuclear development continues to 
require careful evaluation of siting, licensing, construction execution, supply chain, fuel availability, cost, and 
financing.  
 
Small Modular Reactors 
These technologies build upon decades of proven nuclear operating experience while incorporating innovations 
designed to enhance safety, support scalable development through a modular approach, and strengthen 
deployment flexibility, scalability, and operational performance. 
SMRs typically have unit capacities of several hundred megawatts or less, compared to traditional large-scale 
nuclear reactors. This smaller scale can provide planning flexibility by allowing capacity to be added in smaller 
increments than traditional large nuclear projects. SMRs may also be suitable for a broader set of locations, 
including existing nuclear sites, retired or retiring generation sites, industrial areas, and locations closer to major 
load centers. Certain advanced SMR designs also include features such as passive safety systems, alternative 
coolants, higher operating temperatures, or integrated energy storage that may support flexible operation and 
integration with other grid resources. 
The SMR industry has continued to make meaningful progress toward deployment. The NRC has agreed to review 
several new applications including the ESP for Duke Energy’s Belew’s Creek site and phased Construction Permit 
Application for Holtec’s SMR-300 at Palisades. Additionally, major milestones were reached with the completion of 
the environmental assessment of the construction permit application for the Long Mott Generating Station, a 
proposed four-unit X-energy Xe-100 project at Dow’s Seadrift, Texas industrial site and issuance of a construction 
permit for TerraPower’s Kemmerer Power Station Unit 1, the first NRC construction approval for a commercial non-

==== 2026-integrated-resource-plan-update.pdf — page 42 ====
41 
 
light-water reactor in more than 40 years. These milestones demonstrate continued industry progress towards 
commercial deployment of new nuclear.  
Dominion Energy continues to evaluate SMR technologies and potential deployment opportunities and views SMRs, 
including advanced nuclear reactor technologies, as having an important role in future generation portfolios. Since 
the 2025 IRP Update, the Company has furthered its assessment of SMR siting and development considerations at 
the North Anna Power Station. The Company also received SCC approval in July 2026 of its second Rider SMR 
application, enabling recovery of eligible early-stage development costs. In parallel, the Company is evaluating 
potential financing approaches and commercial structures, including arrangements with third parties and large-load 
customers, that may improve project economics and preserve optionality for future SMR development. Depending 
on the outcome of these evaluations, SMR deployment could occur earlier than assumed in the resource portfolios 
presented in this 2026 IRP. 
 
Traditional Scale Reactors 
Traditional large-scale nuclear power plants, such as the Company’s Surry and North Anna nuclear stations, remain 
a proven source of reliable, carbon-free baseload electricity. Large nuclear units can provide substantial quantities 
of firm capacity and energy over long operating lives and can support grid stability, fuel diversity, and 
decarbonization objectives. 
Deploying new traditional large-scale nuclear facilities, however, requires careful evaluation. These projects typically 
require significant land, robust transmission infrastructure, substantial water resources for cooling, extensive 
licensing and permitting, specialized supply chains, and a large long-term capital commitment. The current standard 
10-mile emergency planning zone associated with traditional large light-water reactors may also limit siting flexibility, 
particularly for greenfield locations or sites near population centers. 
Recent U.S. experience demonstrates both the viability and complexity of developing new large-scale nuclear 
generation. The completion of Plant Vogtle Units 3 and 4 confirms that new large-scale nuclear units can be 
constructed and operated in the U.S., while also highlighting the importance of construction execution, supply chain 
maturity, regulatory certainty, and effective project management. Accordingly, traditional large-scale nuclear remains 
a potential long-term resource option and is retained as a selectable resource. However, any future development 
would need to be evaluated in the context of siting, licensing, construction, water supply, transmission, financing, 
and overall customer affordability considerations. 
 
4.5.6  Natural Gas Resources 
Natural gas resources are essential for grid reliability and the energy transition because they are dispatchable 
resources that work in tandem with intermittent renewable generation. Their flexible operating characteristics allow 
them to follow load and generate electricity when it is needed, including during periods of peak demand or when 
renewable resources are unavailable. Natural gas units can quickly start, ramp output up or down, and shut off as 
conditions change, helping to balance large swings in renewable energy production and mitigating the risk of 
intermittent generation to maintain a reliable electric grid. 
As baseload demand continues to grow, additional generation resources will be needed to ensure the electric 
system can reliably meet increasing customer energy requirements. Rising demand places greater pressure on 
existing generation assets and reduces the margin available to respond to peak conditions, equipment outages, or 
fluctuations in renewable energy output. Expanding generation capacity, particularly with dispatchable resources 
that can operate when needed, will help maintain grid reliability, support projected load growth, and ensure 
adequate energy is available under a wide range of operating conditions. 
For future new natural gas facilities, the Company is considering using advanced-class gas turbines to leverage 
their significant advantages because they deliver higher efficiency, lower fuel consumption, and lower emissions

==== 2026-integrated-resource-plan-update.pdf — page 43 ====
42 
 
than traditional turbine technologies. By producing more electricity from the same amount of natural gas, advanced-
class units reduce operating costs and improve market competitiveness, particularly for a baseload facility. Higher 
efficiency also lowers carbon emissions per megawatt-hour, helping support environmental and regulatory 
objectives while maximizing the value of available pipeline gas capacity. Advanced-class turbines are well suited for 
large-scale combined-cycle configurations because their higher output allows a plant to achieve maximum output 
with fewer generating units, reducing overall plant complexity and maintenance requirements. 
The Company is currently considering a combined-cycle (“CC”) approach for new baseload natural gas generation 
facilities. A CC power plant is typically the preferred choice when the system needs a large amount of reliable, 
dispatchable energy that will run frequently throughout the year. Unlike a simple-cycle combustion turbine (“CT”), a 
CC plant captures the exhaust heat from the gas turbines and uses it to produce steam that drives a steam turbine, 
generating additional electricity from the same fuel. This significantly improves efficiency, reduces fuel costs, and 
lowers emissions per megawatt-hour.  
CTs are generally developed when the primary need is peaking capacity, rapid startup capability, or operational 
flexibility rather than low-cost energy production. They are less expensive to construct, can be brought online more 
quickly, and are well suited for serving peak demand periods, supporting renewable integration, and maintaining 
reliability during extreme weather events. For that reason, facilities such as the Chesterfield Energy Reliability 
Center are being developed with simple-cycle CT technology to provide flexible reliability support, while larger 
combined-cycle projects are intended to meet the system’s growing energy requirements over the long term.  
To meet the energy and capacity needs associated with the load forecast, and in the absence of a commercially 
viable carbon-free, dispatchable generation alternative, natural gas generation will remain a critical component of 
the Company's strategy to reliably meet generation demand.  
4.6 Transmission Considerations 
 
4.6.1  Transmission Planning 
Dominion Energy owns the transmission system for the DOM Zone. In addition to the cooperatives dependent on 
the Company’s transmission system, several independent power producers are interconnected with and are 
dependent on the Company’s transmission system for delivery of their capacity and energy into the PJM market. 
Appendix 4P includes additional detail regarding the relationship between the Company and PJM specific to the 
operation and planning of the transmission system. 
4.6.2  Existing and Future Transmission Facilities 
Dominion Energy has approximately 6,800 miles of transmission lines in Virginia, North Carolina, and West Virginia 
at voltages ranging from 69 kV to 500 kV, with these facilities integrated into PJM. Figure 4-12: Dominion Energy's 
Existing Transmission Lines Over 69kV below shows the Company’s existing transmission lines.

The Company is participating in PJM’s latest Open Window, which commenced on July 20, 2026, to identify

expeditiously with PJM, the SCC, local officials, and other stakeholders to fast-track critical projects to ensure 
continued reliability of the transmission system. The Company will continue to evaluate the transmission system and 
plan for the expected load growth. 
For example, during the PJM 2025 RTEP Open Window #1, which ended in August 2025, the PJM Board of 
Managers selected the Company’s proposal for a high voltage direct current (“HVDC”) line. This will be the first 
HVDC proposed for installation in the Company’s territory. Often described as a transmission superhighway, the 
HVDC facility will serve as a major backbone of the grid, enabling the efficient transfer of larger quantities of power 
where and when it is needed most. The project will enhance system reliability, increase transfer capability, support 
integration of new energy resources, and provide greater operational flexibility to meet future load growth. 
During PJM’s evaluation for the 2025 Market Efficiency Open Window, PJM found one congestion driver in the DOM 
Zone to address, which was the result of a buildup of renewables in the area. A 230/115 kV switching station was 
chosen by PJM as the preferred solution.  
The Company also continues to work with PJM to find cost-effective ways to upgrade existing infrastructure on 
existing rights-of-way (i.e., uprates). This approach has led to a significant number of 230 kV line uprates that are in

various stages of engineering and construction. Additionally, the Company continues to evaluate and deploy grid-
enhancing technologies (“GETs”) to improve transmission system capacity and flexibility. Software GETs optimize 
system topology to enhance power flow and reduce congestion while hardware GETs solutions upgrade physical 
assets and infrastructure such as advanced conductors, Flexible Alternating Current Transmission devices, dynamic 
line ratings, and automatic power flow controllers. More details on current and future plans for GETs on the 
transmission network are detailed in Appendix 4P. 
 
4.6.3  Transmission System Reliability Analyses 
The Company continues to conduct reliability analyses to study the impacts of increased demand, increased 
penetration of renewable energy and energy storage resources, and retirement of synchronous generators on the 
transmission system and address any necessary upgrades that may be needed to ensure reliability. The Company 
has included and will continue to include up-to-date reliability analyses in its IRPs and update filings. 
The Company performed the following analyses for this 2026 IRP: (1) an import limit study for the DOM Zone; (2) an 
inertial and frequency response study to evaluate the increasing penetration of inverter-based resources; (3) a 
short-circuit analysis to evaluate the system’s ability to quickly recover from faults; and (4) a review of system 
restoration and black start capabilities.  
In the 2026 IRP, the analyses show that the DOM Zone maintains significant transmission import capability due to 
planned transmission infrastructure additions, while continued reliance on synchronous generation supports 
stronger frequency performance and overall system reliability. The short-circuit study further demonstrated that 
additional synchronous condensers could improve system strength and support the reliable integration of increasing 
levels of inverter-based resources. The system restoration and black-start assessment found that maintaining 
sufficient synchronous and dispatchable generation resources remains critical for restoring the system following a 
widespread outage. Details on the methodologies used for these analyses and their results are provided in 
Appendix 4P. The analyses continue to show that traditional synchronous generation is needed to help maintain 
system reliability. 
In addition, the solar integration cost study evaluated the transmission upgrades and operational requirements 
associated with increasing levels of renewable generation and developed updated cost estimates for integrating 
large-scale solar resources into the transmission system. The study results indicate that transmission upgrades and 
associated costs will be needed when more renewable energy is added into the Dominion Energy system. 
Additional details about this study are provided in Appendix 4Q.

the technology used to monitor, control, and transport energy. The Company will be evaluating how to effectively 
utilize GETs, including sensors, power flow control, and analytical tools. As newer technologies are developed, the 
Company will investigate their potential applicability. See Figure 4-13: GETs Technologies for Transmission and

4.7 Distribution Considerations 
 
As society becomes increasingly dependent on electricity, customers expect higher levels of reliability, resiliency, 
power quality, and service restoration performance. At the same time, the electric distribution system is transforming 
to meet various emerging trends, including accelerated load growth, DERs, transportation electrification, 
digitalization, and evolving customer expectations. These trends require continued modernization of both the 
physical grid and the planning processes used to identify, evaluate, and prioritize investments. Dominion Energy 
continues to advance an integrated distribution planning (“IDP”) framework that evaluates traditional infrastructure 
solutions alongside non-traditional options, including energy storage, demand response, customer-owned resources 
used as non-wires alternatives (“NWAs”), VPPs, grid utilization strategies, and advanced planning and operational 
technologies. 
The Company’s distribution planning process remains consistent with prior IRPs, but it continues to mature through 
implementation of the IDP Roadmap, the Grid Transformation Plan, and related modernization initiatives, including 
deployment of intelligent grid devices, fault location isolation and service restoration (“FLISR”), advanced metering 
infrastructure (“AMI”), volt/var optimization (“VVO”), DERMS functionality, hosting capacity analysis tools, substation 
technology, outage management capabilities, enterprise asset management systems, energy storage pilots, 
microgrid capabilities, and advanced analytics. Collectively, these initiatives improve operational awareness, 
reliability, resilience, DER integration, and customer service while supporting the transition toward a more digital and 
flexible distribution system. 
In addition to core modernization initiatives, the Company is advancing emerging capabilities through pilots, 
operational technologies, and data-driven tools. Examples include expanded remote sensing and image analytics 
through the Image Management and Analytics Program, improved distribution system visibility, enhanced hosting 
capacity analysis, DER management tools, and grid utilization approaches that make better use of existing 
infrastructure, such as non-wires solutions. These emerging capabilities support more efficient planning and 
operations, improve situational awareness, and provide cost-effective solutions to evolving distribution system 
needs. 
Federal and state policy developments further support the Company’s efforts in distribution grid transformation. At 
the federal level, for example, FERC Order 2222 remains an important driver for DER visibility, coordination, and 
operational capability by enabling aggregated DERs—including storage, distributed generation, demand response, 
energy efficiency, thermal storage, electric vehicles, and associated charging equipment—to participate in regional 
wholesale markets. Implementation requires continued coordination among utilities, regional transmission 
organizations, DER aggregators, and customers, as well as investment in DER management systems, processes, 
and supporting technologies. 
At the state level, Virginia continues to support demand flexibility, DER integration, and more efficient grid utilization. 
As discussed above, the SCC recently approved the Company’s VPP Pilot to evaluate how aggregated DERs can 
provide grid services and support system needs during peak demand. The pilot is expected to provide operational 
experience with DER aggregation, customer participation, grid services, and coordination with broader FERC Order 
2222 implementation. The Company is also evaluating demand flexibility and grid utilization concepts that may 
improve asset use while maintaining reliability, resiliency, cybersecurity, and physical security. 
4.7.1  Distribution GETs 
GETs refer to technologies that increase the capacity, flexibility, and efficiency of the existing grid. While GETs are 
often associated with transmission applications such as dynamic line ratings, topology optimization, advanced 
power flow control, and advanced conductors, many distribution modernization initiatives provide similar enabling 
capabilities at the distribution level. For Dominion Energy, distribution-level GETs include technologies such as 
FLISR, VVO, AMI, DERMS, hosting capacity analysis, enterprise asset management systems, and battery energy 
storage systems that can serve as NWAs. These tools enhance operational awareness, improve reliability and 
resiliency, support DER integration, and enable more efficient use of existing distribution assets.

During the 2026 Stakeholder Engagement Process, Stakeholders asked, “How 
are grid-enhancing technologies (GETs) accounted for within the IRP model?” 
 
GETs are not explicitly modeled within the IRP as stand-alone solutions. Their 
inclusion is typically tied to PJM’s identification of specific system constraints and the 
evaluation of solutions to address those needs. Where such constraints and approved 
solutions exist, they are incorporated through the PJM planning inputs used in the 
IRP.

The Company also continues to evaluate advanced conductors for distribution applications. To date, advanced 
conductors have primarily been viewed as a transmission-focused GETs; however, Dominion Energy will continue to 
monitor transmission and distribution applications to determine whether future technical developments, economics, 
operational benefits, or emerging use cases may support broader distribution deployment. 
Looking forward, the Company’s IDP process will continue evaluating infrastructure investments for capacity, 
reliability, asset management, and resiliency needs alongside energy storage, demand response, DERs, NWAs, 
VPPs, GETs, and other innovative grid solutions. Through advanced forecasting, grid modernization programs, 
operational technologies, and data-driven planning tools, the Company seeks to improve grid utilization, facilitate 
DER integration, enhance reliability and resilience, safeguard the electric distribution grid, and provide safe, 
affordable, and increasingly flexible electric service. 
4.8 Environmental Considerations 
 
Environmental regulation remains a key focus in long-term resource planning. Federal and state requirements 
affecting the electric generating sector continue to evolve through rulemaking, reconsideration, litigation, or other 
administrative action.  
Coal-fired, biomass, and natural gas-fired generation continue to support system reliability. Natural gas-fired units, 
particularly simple-cycle combustion turbines, can respond quickly during periods of high demand. Coal and 
biomass units may provide additional operational resilience because they can maintain onsite fuel inventories when 
regional fuel supplies are constrained or curtailed, including during peak winter conditions. State and federal 
developments may affect the dispatch, economics, compliance obligations, and continued operation of these 
resources.  
Several federal regulatory programs are particularly relevant to the Company’s fossil-fueled generating fleet. These 
include the Mercury and Air Toxics Standards rule applicable to coal electric generating units; greenhouse gas 
standards, and emission guidelines established under Sections 111(b) and 111(d) of the Clean Air Act; Effluent 
Limitation Guidelines for wastewater discharges; and Virginia’s CO2 Budget Trading Program, which implements the 
Commonwealth’s participation in RGGI.

==== 2026-integrated-resource-plan-update.pdf — page 50 ====
49 
 
The status and requirements of these programs have changed significantly in recent years and, in some cases, 
remain subject to further administrative or judicial action. Accordingly, the Company considers both current 
environmental requirements and significant regulatory developments that could affect the availability, cost, and 
operation of existing generation and the development of future resources over the IRP planning horizon. See 
Appendix 4R for a summary of environmental regulations. 
4.9 Near-Term Reliability Plan 
 
Dominion Energy is committed to delivering reliable, affordable energy through an “All of the Above” generation 
strategy that utilizes a diverse portfolio of energy resources. Over the next five years, the Company is developing a 
robust action plan to further increase reliability and generation capacity. This effort includes both constructing new 
generating facilities and increasing the Maximum Facility Output as well as Capacity Interconnection Rights (“CIRs”) 
at existing units16 Consistent with this strategy, new natural gas, wind, solar, and energy storage resources will be 
interconnected with PJM to support growing energy needs and strengthen grid reliability.

Chapter 5:  Long-Term Strategic Pathways  
 
Fully Generic IRP Planning 
The resource portfolios presented in this 2026 IRP are based on updated load forecasts, commodity price forecasts, 
technology cost and performance assumptions, environmental and regulatory compliance considerations, and 
resource planning assumptions. Consistent with PJM’s 20-year load forecast planning horizon, the Company 
evaluated portfolios and sensitivities over a 20-year planning period.  
In this 2026 IRP, future generating resources evaluated within the modeled portfolios are represented as generic 
resource additions (i.e., they no longer include specific projects referenced in the RPS Development Plan cases). 
This change reflects the distinct purposes between the IRP and the Company’s RPS Development Plan filing. As 
explained above, while the IRP evaluates long-term resource needs and compares alternative portfolios under a 
range of future conditions, it does not request approval of specific generation projects. Conversely, project-specific 
resource proposals and supporting information related to compliance with the RPS Program are presented through 
separate regulatory proceedings. Accordingly, future resources shown in this IRP should be viewed as illustrative 
planning constructs used to evaluate system needs and portfolio performance rather than as specific facilities 
proposed for development. Information related to the Company’s RPS Program compliance activities and 
associated resource proposals can be found in Case No. PUR-2025-00148. The North Carolina Clean Energy and 
Energy Efficiency Portfolio Standard Compliance Plan will be filed contemporaneously with this IRP pursuant to 
NCUC Rule R8-67(b)(2). Additional information regarding considerations in this IRP is provided in Chapter 4: Key 
Planning Assumptions.

5.2.1  Summary of Portfolio Modeling Assumptions 
As stated in Chapter 5.1, the resource portfolios presented in this 2026 IRP are based on updated load forecasts, 
commodity price forecasts, and generation cost assumptions. See Appendix 1 for a summary of modeling 
assumptions associated with each portfolio. In addition, each portfolio includes a high-level summary of 
assumptions at the beginning of each portfolio description. See Chapter 4.8 Environmental Considerations for a 
summary of environment assumptions associated with this IRP. 
 
5.2.2  Resource Build Limits 
Resource build limits are used in the IRP to reflect real-world constraints and ensure the model produces practical, 
implementable results. The Company develops build limit assumptions that allow the model to evaluate portfolios 
capable of meeting applicable VCEA and RPS Program requirements where required to do so, while also reflecting 
realistic deployment constraints. These limits can represent factors such as supply chain considerations, siting and 
permitting timelines, interconnection requirements, and the pace at which new resources can realistically be 
developed and integrated onto the system. See Chapter 4.5 for more detailed information on factors that impact 
build limit considerations.

5.2.3.1  Retirement Analysis 
The VCEA mandates the retirement of carbon-emitting generation by the end of 2045 unless the Company petitions, 
and the SCC finds that a given retirement would threaten the reliability and security of electric service to customers. 
Separate from these mandates, the Company completed two analyses related to retirement of existing units. First, 
the Company completed a 20-year cash flow analysis focused on coal-fired, biomass-fired, and large CC generation 
facilities under market conditions. For the 2026 IRP, the Company evaluated 20-year cash flows under the 
Company Preferred Plan. Unit NPVs were derived by comparing the unit costs, including operations and 
maintenance and capital, to the total forecasted unit benefits, consisting of energy and capacity revenues (and REC 
revenues, where applicable) for the next 20 years based on the snapshot in time when the analysis was conducted. 
The results of the 20-year cash flow analysis are included in Figure 5-4: 20-year cash flow retirement analysis (in

Second, as directed by the SCC, the Company included the same unit-specific data for the units listed in Figure 5-4 
in PLEXOS to allow the model to optimize the timing of unit retirements. The Company presents these results as 
part of the Company Preferred Plan, which shows all units running through the Planning Period (i.e., through 2046). 
A positive NPV result indicates that the unit’s revenues exceed its fixed and variable costs, while a negative value 
indicates the unit’s revenues are expected to be below its fixed and variable costs. All units in this analysis have a 
positive NPV and PLEXOS did not choose to economically retire any units. This analysis allows the Company to 
view each unit’s near-term projected revenue and cost streams in one place, and to determine key drivers for unit 
profitability. It is worth noting that a 20-year cash flow analysis is not the only deciding factor in retiring an existing 
resource. Other quantitative and qualitative considerations must be prudently factored into such determinations, 
such as remaining useful life, capacity and energy replacements, system reliability, fuel contracts, transmission 
system considerations, personnel, impact of continued operation of the unit(s) on the local economy, and pending 
environmental regulations, to name a few. Modeling in this 2026 IRP is based on normal weather and models the 
complete system, which does not fully capture the value of a unit that may be based on location, fuel diversity, value 
in extreme weather scenarios, operational flexibility, and black-start capability, among other factors. The Company 
has not made any decision regarding the retirement of any current generating unit and does not currently anticipate 
any such retirements before 2045. Appendix 4K-6 lists the generating units considered for potential retirement in 
the Company Preferred Plan. 
 
5.2.3.2  Sensitivity Analyses on the Company Preferred Plan 
The Company conducted sensitivity analyses for this 2026 IRP to show the potential paths forward under different 
future conditions consistent with SCC and NCUC requirements. These sensitivities are listed in Table 2-1: Market 
Scenarios, Portfolios, and Cases, and include the following: 
• High Load Forecast 
• Low Load Forecast 
• Company Load Forecast 
• Least-Cost RPS 
• High Fuel Prices

62 
 
• Low Fuel Prices 
• High Capital Construction Cost 
• Low Capital Construction Cost 
 
Plan Sensitivities on Load Forecast 
First, the Company conducted sensitivities using different load forecasts. The Company used the same general 
methodology to create the high/low sensitivities as it did in the PJM Derived Load Forecast. The differences are that 
the high/low sensitivities use a variation on the Data Center Load Forecast and the EE adjustment to the load 
forecast. In the high load forecast sensitivity, the Company scaled the PJM Data Center Load Forecast such that it 
was consistent with the Company’s internal 95
th percentile data center forecast. Additionally, the Company modeled 
that EE savings would be half of the forecasted amounts. This resulted in a high load forecast sensitivity that starts 
out 3% higher than the PJM Derived Load Forecast in the first year, moving to 14% higher by 2040. 
The low load forecast sensitivity used the same general methodology as in the high load forecast sensitivity, with the 
exception that the PJM Data Center Load Forecast was scaled to be consistent with the Company’s internal 5
th 
percentile data center forecast. Similarly, EE savings were increased by 50%. This resulted in a low load forecast 
sensitivity that starts off 2% lower than the PJM Derived Load Forecast in the first year, moving to 13% lower by 
2040.  
In addition, the Company also ran a sensitivity using the 2026 Company Load Forecast. Figure 5-5: Total MW 
Addition Comparison: Load Forecast Sensitivities shows the results of these sensitivities. Cost summaries are 
included in the following section.

The High, Low, and Company Load Forecast Sensitivities are instructive regarding the potential differentiation in 
resource needs depending on customer demand. As would be expected, additional resources are needed in the 
High Load sensitivity, with the model selecting additional storage and nuclear resources relative to the Company 
Preferred Plan. In the Low Load sensitivity, the model optimizes by building fewer natural gas and nuclear 
resources, but incrementally more storage to replace some of the needed capacity. Finally, the Company Load 
Forecast results in only a 200 MW difference in resource additions via incremental storage than the Company 
Preferred Plan, though as can be more fully observed in Appendix 1, energy requirements in this sensitivity are also 
lower, resulting in lower overall system costs. Total Portfolio Cost comparisons for these sensitivities as well as 
additional sensitivities adjusting commodity price assumptions are addressed in the next section.

The Forced Retirements by 2045 Portfolio retires all Company owned carbon-emitting resources in the 
Commonwealth, with the exception of the Company’s biomass units that are not subject to the VCEA, by the end of 
2045. For this portfolio, multiple modeling assumptions, in contrast to the Company Preferred Plan, were made to 
derive a case that would fully meet customer requirements. These assumptions included:  
• Doubling the build limit for solar from 1,200 MW to 2,400 MW annually; 
• Doubling the build limit for SMR nuclear units, by eliminating the every-other-year constraint; 
• The Company would continue operating the three existing units at its Mount Storm Power Station located in 
West Virginia (as this power station is located outside Virginia, it does not fall within the purview of the 
VCEA);  
• The model could select an additional pair of combined cycle generation resources outside of the 
Commonwealth that would not retire by 2045;  
• The model was constrained so that no new gas units could be selected after 2035; and 
• Appropriate location(s) would be available within the Commonwealth to build new large-scale nuclear units.

HB 895/SB 448 significantly expanded the energy storage deployment targets for the Company, including adding 
new requirements for long-duration energy storage targets. Under the amended statute, the Company must petition 
for 16,000 MW of short-duration energy storage resources by 2045; 4,000 MW of which must be petitioned for by 
2030. Additionally, the Company must petition for 4,000 MW of long-duration energy storage resources—defined as 
resources with 10 or more hours of capacity—by 2045, half of which must be petitioned for by 2035. Notably, 
pursuant to Enactment Clause 4 of HB 895/SB 448, the long-duration energy storage target does not become 
effective until the SCC determines that the technology and procurement targets are technically viable and 
reasonably achievable. The SCC must issue its determination in that proceeding by March 1, 2031, and may 
propose modified targets and interim targets for long-duration energy storage. Additionally, during that same 
proceeding, the SCC must review the short-duration energy storage targets and may adjust the targets based on the 
status of available energy storage technologies and the benefits of energy storage to customers and to the security 
and reliability of the electric grid.  
Like the Company Preferred Plan, the Forced Full Storage Portfolio pre-programs into the model the deployment of 
4 GW of short-duration battery storage that is petitioned for by 2030, taking into consideration the capacity that has 
already been petitioned for in the Company’s Clean Energy filings. Beyond that, the Company also pre-programs an 
additional 12 GW of short-duration battery storage (less certain capacity designed for behind-the-meter or grid 
transformation projects under the legislation) and 4 GW of long-duration battery storage by 2045. In total, this 
portfolio builds 14.5 GW of energy storage across the Planning Period. This Portfolio still requires an additional 21.5 
GW of solar, 3.4 GW of wind, 7 GW of natural gas, and 1.3 GW of nuclear resources to meet customer needs, 
which were economically selected by the model.

5.3 Locational Model  
 
In its Final Order in Case No. PUR-2024-00184 (the 2024 IRP), the SCC directed that "[i]n modeling Dominion’s 
next IRP, Dominion and [VA] Staff shall work together to develop a locational model in PLEXOS using no more than 
four (4) Virginia-specific regional nodes."22 Consistent with that directive, the Company has developed a locational 
modeling framework and presents the results of that effort in this 2026 IRP. 
The Company engaged in a series of collaborative discussions with VA Staff, including alignment on the scope and 
design of the locational model. As agreed with VA Staff, the locational model applies four nodes to a single portfolio: 
(1) DOM LSE North, (2) DOM LSE South, (3) non-DOM LSE/PJM market node to the north (“Market North”), and 
non-DOM LSE/PJM market node to the south (“Market South”), with the James River serving as the conceptual 
dividing line. Transfers among these nodes are constrained by three transmission “pipes,” and the analysis 
incorporates zonal build limits and the PJM-derived DOM LSE Load Forecast allocated between the northern and 
southern zones based on the split forecast in the Company Load Forecast. The dividing line itself was refined to 
include a transmission capacity study of major wires crossing between the zones and a GIS-based allocation of 
load, including data center demand. PLEXOS was then used to model a resulting least-cost expansion plan. 
The resulting 20-year expansion plan totals approximately 41.1 GW of new capacity through 2046. Relative to the 
Company Preferred Plan, the locational model selects approximately 1,900 MW of additional energy storage—
concentrated in the South, where solar could otherwise be curtailed—one additional SMR in the North, and no 
incremental onshore wind, while holding natural gas additions constant. These results, together with the underlying 
assumptions, are described in the sections that follow. 
Description of Locational Model  
As noted above, the locational model uses a north-south dividing line primarily based on the major transmission 
corridors that exist within DOM Zone. At a high level, that dividing line exists roughly along the path of the James 
River. The final “line” is depicted in Figure 5-24: Locational Model Illustrative Visual. 
 
22 2024 IRP Final Order at 6.

==== 2026-integrated-resource-plan-update.pdf — page 84 ====
83 
 
Figure 5-24: Locational Model Illustrative Visual 
 
A zonal load forecast was developed for the DOM LSE North and DOM LSE South nodes and apportioned existing 
customer load between those zones. As of 2025, DOM LSE load on an energy and demand basis is located 
approximately 70% in DOM LSE North and 30% in DOM LSE South. On a 10-, 15-, and 20-year basis, peak and 
energy grow faster in the North, which shifts the load share northward as load grows during the study period. Figure 
5-25: Zonal Load Forecast CAGR Comparison shows these comparisons. 
Figure 5-25: Zonal Load Forecast CAGR Comparison

To set up the PLEXOS modeling, the Company assigned all existing generation to either the DOM LSE North or 
DOM LSE South node. Finally, the Company established nodal build limits for the expansion plan. The Company 
analyzed whether, as part of the build limits, different cost assumptions for future generic resources were 
appropriate. Based on the Company’s experience, as well as a review of actual costs for the Company’s Clean 
Energy projects, it was determined that a cost differential was not appropriate at this time.

==== 2026-integrated-resource-plan-update.pdf — page 85 ====
84 
 
The locational model pre-programs the same VCEA-prescribed quantities of solar and storage resources as 
reflected in the Company’s Preferred Plan. The locational model also uses the same annual and cumulative build 
limits as used in the Company’s Preferred Plan, apportioned as follows: 
• 25% to DOM LSE North / 75% of utility-scale solar offered to DOM LSE South 
• Energy storage was offered to both DOM LSE North and DOM LSE South up to 175 MW/year each 
• All wind (onshore and offshore) was offered only to DOM LSE South 
• Natural gas combined cycles were offered one unit each in DOM LSE North and DOM LSE South 
• Natural gas combustion turbines were offered to each node up to the cumulative limit 
• Nuclear units (SMRs and large-scale) were offered to each node up to the cumulative limits 
The Company based its solar apportionment on actual experience with its annual Clean Energy / Renewable 
Portfolio Standards projects. For CE-1 through CE-6, approximately 75% of the Company-owned solar resources 
have been located in what was designed as the DOM LSE South Node and approximately 80% of the third-party 
PPAs have been located in DOM LSE South. While this may not always be the case—particularly over a 20-year 
horizon—the Company applied the simplifying assumption that projects would be similarly available during the study 
period. The determination to locate wind in DOM LSE South was based on the likely interconnection points of any 
future offshore wind installations as well as the availability of development areas for onshore wind. 
 
Summary of Locational Model Results  
The resulting 20-year expansion plan for the Locational Model totals approximately 41.1 GW of new capacity 
through 2046. Relative to the Company Preferred Plan, the Locational Model selects approximately 1,900 MW of 
additional energy storage—concentrated in the South, where solar could otherwise be curtailed—one additional 
SMR in the North, and no incremental onshore wind, while holding natural gas additions constant. The decline in 
solar capacity is due to modeling set-up in enforcing a 75/25 split rather than a different optimization preference.

The full Locational Model results are provided in Appendix 1. As seen in the full Locational Model results, net energy 
purchases (GWh) are materially higher in the Locational Model than in the Company Preferred Plan. This likely 
reflects that there were hours where load in DOM LSE North exceeded the generation that could be delivered via 
the South-North transmission “pipe” as well as the generation available to dispatch in DOM LSE North, forcing the 
model to make market purchases when it otherwise would not have if Company-owned or controlled generation 
were available. Within the modeling results, the Company further observed that solar capacity factors in DOM LSE 
South did begin to decline around 2040 as some solar generation is curtailed in hours where DOM LSE South load 
in combination with transfer capability was insufficient. These results emphasize the need for the Company to 
continue investing in transmission infrastructure to move energy throughout the DOM Zone in response to 
customers’ energy needs. The Company will continue to pursue development and third-party power purchase 
opportunities in the northern portion of the Company’s service territory, though such opportunities have historically 
been limited.

direction, and explainable on the basis of the locational constraints introduced into the model: Additional energy 
storage is selected in the DOM LSE South node to absorb solar output that would otherwise be curtailed; onshore 
wind is displaced at the margin; and one additional small modular reactor is selected in the DOM LSE North node, 
where load is more concentrated and transfer capability is more limited. The Company will need to continue to 
invest in significant transmission infrastructure over the next 20 years to move energy throughout the DOM Zone. 
Generation sited in the North and closer to load could be preferred over more rural locations if it is available, which it 
has not been historically either through self-development opportunities or through third-party market offers. The 
Locational Model produced no anomalous, counterintuitive, or otherwise surprising outcomes. The Company 
therefore submits that the locational modeling exercise, while considerably more complex than the Company's 
traditional zonal approach, serves principally to confirm the reasonableness of the Company Preferred Plan rather 
than to suggest a materially different resource strategy. The results also do not support transitioning to a fully 
location-specific modeling approach in future IRPs.

Chapter 6:  Customer Resources & Education  
 
6.1 Environmental Justice 
 
The Company remains committed to making environmental justice (“EJ”) considerations part of our everyday 
decision-making as we work to deliver reliable, affordable, and increasingly clean energy to our customers in 
Virginia and North Carolina. The Company continues to follow its EJ policy and the Virginia Environmental Justice 
Act (“VEJA”) in its reviews for all major projects.  
Dominion Energy’s EJ Policy 
In 2018, the Company adopted an EJ policy. Under this policy, project development teams are required to consult 
with the Company’s dedicated EJ specialists who conduct EJ reviews for all major projects, regardless of whether it 
is required for permitting or other regulatory approvals. 
The Company’s EJ evaluations begin as early as feasible in the project development cycle. The Company identifies 
potentially disadvantaged or marginalized segments of the community near a potential project site according to 
statutory definitions and designs an outreach plan to equitably solicit meaningful feedback from all interested 
community members. The Company’s outreach efforts include the project development and construction team, 
communications staff, and permitting experts who all work together to ensure information is available, questions are 
answered, and feedback from the community is considered.  
The Company works closely with all appropriate federal, state, local, and tribal agencies to mitigate environmental 
impacts through the required permitting, approval, or consultation processes.

==== 2026-integrated-resource-plan-update.pdf — page 89 ====
88 
 
The Virginia Environmental Justice Act 
The VEJA sets the policy of Virginia to promote EJ, ensuring the fair treatment and meaningful involvement of every 
person—regardless of race, color, national origin, income, faith, or disability—regarding the development, 
implementation, or enforcement of any environmental law, regulation, or policy.  
Using data from VDEQ’s EJScreen+ website, a Company analysis finds VEJA definitions identify approximately 
80% of the Commonwealth’s land area as meeting EJ community definitions, and approximately 86% of the 
Commonwealth’s population currently live in an area of the Commonwealth that meets EJ community definitions. 
With such a large proportion of the Commonwealth defined through the VEJA as an EJ Community, avoidance is 
not possible. Figure 6-1: VEJA EJ Community Map with the Company’s Generation Resources shows the 
Company’s generation resources along with the geographic areas that meet the definition of EJ community in 2026. 
 
Figure 6-1: VEJA EJ Community Map with the Company’s Generation Resources 
 
Considering Environmental Justice  
Generally, evaluation of environmental justice involves consideration of a variety of case-specific factors, including 
(1) the type of project or program at issue; (2) where it will occur; (3) what type of environmental impacts are likely; 
(4) if any impacts, whether they are significantly negative or adverse; and, (5) whether there are EJ communities 
that might suffer the adverse environmental impacts of the proposed activity. The Company follows its established

==== 2026-integrated-resource-plan-update.pdf — page 90 ====
89 
 
EJ review process when evaluating specific projects and programs and presents the results of the review in the 
relevant proceedings before the SCC. The Company will also present its evaluation as appropriate in relevant 
proceedings before the NCUC. 
Importantly, a reliable and affordable energy grid is essential to a healthy environment for any community, as are the 
economic development opportunities contingent upon the same. The transition to a clean-energy future will require 
substantial development of new infrastructure across the Commonwealth. The public need for new infrastructure 
and the potential harm done by selecting a “no action,” more costly, or less reliable alternative must be weighed 
against the possible outcomes for local communities resulting from any proposed project. 
The Company believes that whether a proposed action promotes EJ is best evaluated on a case-by-case basis, 
informed by the location of the project in question and project-specific characteristics. The Company has established 
an EJ review process for evaluating its specific projects and programs consistent with relevant laws and regulations. 
Based on this, the Company presents the results of these project-specific review processes in the relevant 
proceedings before the SCC, such as in its applications to construct new generating facilities or new or rebuilt 
transmission lines, and will do so as appropriate in relevant proceedings before the NCUC.  
As demonstrated in this IRP, meeting customers’ needs will require an “All of the Above” strategy with a portfolio of 
diverse resources. As the Company’s generation portfolio changes, commitments to workforce development and the 
communities in which it operates continue. 
The Company is working to attract, retain, and retrain employees for careers that span different technologies, 
including renewables, storage, and new nuclear. The Company’s Education Assistance Program provides tuition 
reimbursement for employees to gain the necessary education to transition to clean-energy jobs. While the 
Company has not made any decision regarding the retirement of any current generating unit, any future retirement 
decision will be handled in accordance with the communication requirements in Va. Code § 56-599 C.  
In addition to helping employees, the Company will continue to support the communities in which it operates and 
hopes to continue operating for many years. For example, the Company continues to focus on the development of 
clean energy on brownfield sites, which will result in continued tax support to localities if a fossil fuel facility retires. 
6.2 Customer Education 
 
The Company is committed to providing information to its customers about their energy consumption and how to 
manage their costs, empowering them to take advantage of the numerous enhanced capabilities enabled by the 
Grid Transformation Plan and other initiatives.  
The Company’s customer education initiatives include providing demand and energy usage information, educational 
opportunities, and online support options to assist customers in managing their energy consumption and taking 
advantage of new incentives and offerings. The educational initiatives apply to the Company’s customers in both 
Virginia and North Carolina.  
Dominion Energy understands the economic pressures on our customers and recognizes that energy costs are an 
important concern. While economic market conditions, weather patterns, technological advances and other factors 
are generally outside of the Company’s control, our customers experience their effects directly. The Company 
therefore remains focused on the factors within its control, including disciplined planning and operations, prudent 
management of costs, and investments designed to support reliable service while managing long-term customer 
impacts. Consistent with its focus on affordability, the Company also offers a variety of programs and resources to 
help our customers save energy, manage their bills, and access assistance when needed.

==== 2026-integrated-resource-plan-update.pdf — page 91 ====
90 
 
Helping Customers Save and Manage their Bill 
The Company has established a dedicated portal on its website at www.dominionenergy.com/savemore to help 
customers find ways to save energy and manage their bill. The site takes customers through an Energy Savings 
Finder tool that links them to the resources they need based on their circumstances. Available resources fall into 
three main categories:  
• Bill management tools, such as budget billing and energy alerts; 
• Programs to help customers save energy and money, through energy efficiency and demand response; and 
• Bill payment and crisis assistance for qualifying households. 
Economic Development Rates (for qualifying customers)   
As of October 2026, the Company has eight customer accounts in Virginia receiving service under economic 
development rates. The total load associated with these rates is approximately 93.7 MW. As of October 2026, the 
Company has no customers in North Carolina receiving service under an economic development rate.  
Website and Supporting Print Collateral   
The Dominion Energy website—https://www.dominionenergy.com—serves as a central hub for public education. 
The Company offers program- and project-specific information, fact sheets, brochures, videos, and other supporting 
documents to provide background and updates on the benefits and enhanced capabilities associated with various 
investments and initiatives. These include, but are not limited to, approved elements of the Grid Transformation 
Plan, major infrastructure projects, and new offerings such as rates, tools, and mobile apps as they become 
available.  
Social Media 
The Company uses the social media channels of X® and Meta® to provide real-time updates on energy-related 
topics, promote Company messages, and provide two-way communication with customers. The Company also 
manages pages on YouTube® and Instagram for further outreach to the general public, residential customers, and 
business customers. LinkedIn® is leveraged for reaching commercial and industrial customers.  
• The Company’s X® account is available online at: https://x.com/dominionenergy.  
• The Company’s Facebook® account is available online at: https://www.facebook.com/dominionenergy. 
• The Company’s YouTube® account is available online at https://www.youtube.com/dominionenergy.  
• The Company’s Instagram® account is available online at https://www.instagram.com/dominionenergy/.  
• The Company’s LinkedIn® account is available online at 
https://www.linkedin.com/company/dominionenergy/.  
News Releases 
The Company prepares news releases and reports on the latest developments regarding its customer-facing 
initiatives and provides updates on Company offerings and recommendations for saving energy as new information 
and programs become available. Current and archived news releases can be viewed at: 
https://news.dominionenergy.com/.  
Energy Conservation Programs 
The Company’s website has a section dedicated to energy conservation that contains helpful information for both 
residential and non-residential customers, including information about the Company’s DSM programs. Dozens of 
programs are featured on the website, and include eligibility guidelines, program details, steps to enroll, and 
success stories, as well as contact information to speak with program specialists. Through consumer education 
using a variety of channels to reach multiple customer classes, the Company is working to encourage the adoption 
of energy-efficient technologies in residences and businesses in Virginia and North Carolina. A multi-channel 
marketing strategy, including radio, print, digital, and out-of-home channels helps drive adoption, education, and

==== 2026-integrated-resource-plan-update.pdf — page 92 ====
91 
 
awareness of the Company’s DSM programs. A website for programs in Virginia is maintained at 
https://www.dominionenergy.com/virginia/save-energy. A website for programs in North Carolina is available at 
https://www.dominionenergy.com/north-carolina/save-energy.  
Community Outreach – Trade Shows, Exhibits, and Speaking Engagements 
Dominion Energy conducts outreach seminars and speaking engagements to share relevant energy conservation 
program information to both residential and commercial audiences. The Company also participates in various trade 
shows, exhibits and community events to educate customers on the Company’s programs and inform customers 
and communities about the importance of implementing energy-saving measures in homes and businesses and 
taking advantage of new rates and offerings as they become available. Company representatives positively impact 
the communities the Company serves through presentations to elementary, middle, and high school students about 
its programs, wise energy use, and environmental stewardship. Additional partnerships with the educational 
community are offered through mentoring initiatives, philanthropic support, and other means to strengthen science, 
technology, engineering, and mathematics competitiveness to help prepare students for tomorrow’s careers. 
Information on educational grants, scholarships, and programs for teachers and students is available on the 
Company’s website at: https://www.dominionenergy.com/about/our-company/customers-and-community.

Order / Guideline Requirement 2026 IRP Section 
Va. Code § 56-599 (D) As part of preparing any integrated resource plan pursuant to this section, each 
utility shall conduct outreach to engage the public in a stakeholder review process 
and provide opportunities for the public to contribute information, input, and idea's 
on the utility's integrated resource plan, including the plan's development 
methodology, modeling inputs, and assumptions, as well as the ability for the public 
to make relevant inquiries, to the utility when formulating its integrated resource 
plan. Each utility shall report its public outreach efforts to the Commission. The 
stakeholder review process shall include representatives from multiple interest 
groups, including residential and industrial classes of ratepayers. Each utility shall, at 
the time of the filing of its integrated resource plan, report on any stakeholder 
meetings that have occurred prior to the filing date.

Order / Guideline Requirement 2026 IRP Section 
Case No. PUR-2020-00035 
Final Order at 14 and n.56 
Dominion proposes that future IRPs and updates include a least cost VCEA plan that 
would meet (i) applicable carbon regulations and (ii) the mandatory RPS Program 
requirements of the VCEA. For this plan, the Company proposes not to force the 
model to select any specific resource nor exclude any reasonable resource and allow 
the model to optimize the accompanying resource plan. Based on the record in this 
proceeding, we find this proposal to be reasonable at this time. While the 
Commission recognizes that certain build constraints may be necessary under 
certain circumstances, the reasonableness of any such build constraints will be 
subject to Commission review in future proceedings.

Preferred Plan

Chapter 6.1 
Environmental Justice 
Case No. PUR-2020-00035 
Final Order at 15-16 
The Commission will require Dominion to file an updated bill analysis by plan in 
future IRPs and updates with the following modifications:  
• The Company shall provide bill impacts over the next ten years for the least cost 
VCEA plan, the Company's preferred plan, and any additional plans presented, 
including residential, small general service and large general service customer bills. 
Each update shall include an additional year of projections beyond 2030 as each year 
passes and should consistently be compared back to the actual bill as of May 1, 
2020. 
• As proposed by Staff, the Company shall use class allocation factors and projected 
sales recently used to set rate adjustment clause rates in the bill analysis. 
• In addition to projections, the analysis shall include actual bill impact information 
as each year passes. For example, in the 2021 update filing, the Company would 
include the actual bill information as of December 31, 2020 in the bill analysis.
