Appendix 2A: Stakeholder Engagement Process Report

==== 2026-integrated-resource-plan-update.pdf — page 112 ====
2 
 
Background  
In 2023, the Virginia General Assembly enacted legislation that, among other provisions, directed 
Virginia Electric and Power Company (“Dominion Energy” or the “Company”), when preparing its 
Integrated Resource Plan (“IRP”), to “engage the public in a stakeholder review process and provide 
opportunities for the public to contribute information, input, and ideas, including the plan’s 
development methodology, modeling inputs, and assumptions, as well as the ability for the public to 
make relevant inquiries.”1  
  
In 2024, the Company conducted its first IRP stakeholder process and conducted a subsequent IRP 
stakeholder process for the 2025 update year. Utilizing feedback from stakeholders and lessons 
learned from prior years, the Company refined its approach for 2026 by focusing stakeholder 
meetings on topics critical to this year’s IRP and on input needed from stakeholders to develop the 
Stakeholder Input Case. This year’s meetings, which were a mix of hybrid and virtual-only, were 
aligned with key internal planning milestones, allowing stakeholders to provide timely feedback on 
modeling assumptions, scenario development, and resource options under consideration. This 
approach helped ensure that stakeholder perspectives were meaningfully considered in the 2026 
IRP. 
 
At the end of 2025, the Company issued a request for proposals (“RFP”) to hire a third-party, neutral 
facilitator for the 2026 Stakeholder Engagement Process. While hiring a third-party facilitator was not 
required for the 2026 process, the Company recognizes it will be a requirement for all future IRPs, 
due to new legislation passed by the Virginia General Assembly.
2 Through the RFP, the Company 
received bids from five vendors and scored each interested vendor based on their prior facilitation 
experience, ability to be neutral, and proposed cost, among other variables. The Company retained 
the Great Plains Institute (“GPI”) to facilitate neutral and fair discussions between the Company and 
stakeholders for the 2026 Stakeholder Engagement Process.  
  
In this Stakeholder Process Report (“Report”), Dominion Energy outlines its stakeholder 
engagement efforts and describes how it worked to involve a broad array of stakeholders and their 
perspectives throughout the development of the 2026 IRP. The Report also includes a narrative 
summary of the feedback received – both quantitative and qualitative – that informed the 
Stakeholder Input Case for the 2026 IRP. 
  
This Report, while reflective of the Company’s efforts, is solely the work of Dominion Energy and 
does not represent the view or endorsement of any participating stakeholders, nor our facilitators. In 
addition to this Report, there is an Engagement Summary Report from GPI (“Facilitator Report”), 
found in Appendix 2B, to summarize the stakeholder process and the methods used to gather 
stakeholder input from the perspective of the facilitator. The Company recognizes stakeholder 
engagement is an evolving process and remains committed to continuous improvement in future IRP 
cycles to better reflect stakeholder priorities and policy developments. 
  
 
 
1 This requirement is codified at Va. Code § 56-599 D. 
2 See Va. Code § 56-599 D.

==== 2026-integrated-resource-plan-update.pdf — page 113 ====
3 
 
Stakeholder Identification 
To identify potential interested stakeholders for the 2026 Stakeholder Engagement Process, 
Dominion Energy utilized its 2025 stakeholder list, which included participants from past IRP 
proceedings; staff from the Virginia State Corporation Commission (“SCC”) and North Carolina 
Utilities Commission (“NCUC”); other local, state, and federal officials; non-governmental 
organizations; tribal nations; nonprofit groups; the military and defense sector; labor unions; 
businesses and large energy users; and individual citizens, among others.  
  
To expand outreach and encourage participation from new stakeholders, the Company published 
public notices in 26 newspapers in Virginia and 24 newspapers in North Carolina. These notices 
were strategically placed to reach a broad geographic and demographic audience, including 
underserved and rural communities. 
  
Figure 1: Sample of Public Notice 
 
  
In total, as of the August 14, 2026 stakeholder meeting, approximately 110 individual stakeholders, 
including 61 unique organizations, have participated in the 2026 IRP Stakeholder Engagement 
Process. A list of organizations that participated in at least one stakeholder meeting can be found in 
the Facilitator Report in Appendix 2B.  
  
Stakeholder Process Design 
Drawing on experiences from previous stakeholder processes, the Company planned a series of 
stakeholder meetings intended to solicit meaningful dialogue and feedback from participants. In 
designing this year’s process, the Company collaborated with GPI to create an accessible and 
productive process for an audience of stakeholders with a range of existing IRP knowledge.

==== 2026-integrated-resource-plan-update.pdf — page 114 ====
4 
 
Throughout the meetings, the Company maintained a stakeholder process website, 
https://devirp.dominionenergy.com/. There, stakeholders had access to meeting materials, meeting 
recordings, and could view questions and answers from previous meetings. Stakeholders could also 
use the website to ask questions directly to the Company. Questions received on the website were 
posted publicly for other stakeholders to view. Additionally, the Company requested GPI to create a 
dedicated email inbox to allow direct communication between the facilitator and stakeholders.  
 
As in previous years, the Company issued two key surveys to solicit direct stakeholder feedback. 
First, the Company issued a Stakeholder Interest Survey prior to the kickoff meeting to gauge 
participants’ interest in a variety of topics. This survey helped the Company and GPI identify which 
topics were most important to stakeholders. These topics then became the focus of various 
meetings throughout the stakeholder process. Second, in partnership with GPI and stakeholders, the 
Company designed the Stakeholder Input Case Survey. This survey was utilized to determine the 
inputs that would be used to create the Stakeholder Input Case.  
 
Unlike previous years, this year, the Company provided two distinct styles of meetings: IRP 
conferences and modeling meetings. The IRP conferences were designed as longer form 
educational meetings and were geared toward an audience with a range of existing IRP knowledge. 
The modeling meetings were designed to provide a deeper dive into modeling topics and were 
geared toward stakeholders with prior modeling expertise. All stakeholders were able to participate 
in both the IRP conferences and modeling meetings. 
 
In total, the Company held 7 meetings, totaling over 12 hours of direct engagement, and responded 
to more than 188 questions from stakeholders. The Company will host a final “Post-Filing Meeting” 
on October 21, 2026, to share the 2026 IRP filed with both the SCC and NCUC. 
 
Figure 2 shows the breakdown of meetings and surveys conducted during the 2026 Stakeholder 
Engagement Process. For a detailed summary of each meeting from the perspective of the 
facilitator, please reference the Facilitator Report in Appendix 2B.

==== 2026-integrated-resource-plan-update.pdf — page 115 ====
5 
 
Figure 2: 2026 Stakeholder Process Engagement Schedule 
 
 
 
 
Stakeholder Survey Results 
As with previous IRP Stakeholder Engagement Processes, the Company hosted these stakeholder 
meetings with the end goal of creating a Stakeholder Input Case to include as a separate portfolio in 
our filing. To determine the inputs selected for this year’s Stakeholder Input Case, the Company, in 
collaboration with GPI and stakeholders, designed a Stakeholder Input Case Survey. For a detailed 
review of this survey and its results, please see the Facilitator Report in Appendix 2B. Below is an 
image that summarizes the results of the Stakeholder Input Case Survey.

==== 2026-integrated-resource-plan-update.pdf — page 116 ====
6 
 
Figure 3: Results of the Stakeholder Input Case Survey 
 
 
Stakeholders were presented with the survey results on August 14, 2026. The results of the survey 
showed that the respondents were generally aligned in some areas, like compliance with the Virginia 
Clean Economy Act (“VCEA”) and nuclear resources, and diverged on other topics, like fossil-fuel 
retirements and offshore wind resources. A sample of some survey results are described below: 
• In general, a majority of stakeholders agreed that the Stakeholder Input Case should follow 
all aspects of the VCEA. Specifically, 55% of stakeholders wanted the model to be pre-
programmed to follow the minimum development and ownership targets outlined in the 
VCEA. Additionally, 55% of stakeholders declined to include fossil units, like natural gas, as 
a selectable resource for the model. Notably, 45% of stakeholders agreed that fossil fuel 
units should be selected on an economic basis but diverged on specific build limits for the 
model.  
• Stakeholders were divided on how to handle retirements. Only 47% of stakeholders agreed 
that retirements should follow the forced-retirement pathway outlined in the VCEA. 37% of 
stakeholders requested the model to retire fossil fuel units on an economic, or “least-cost 
optimized” basis.   
• Stakeholders were aligned on the use of nuclear energy as a selectable resource for the 
model. In fact, 84% of stakeholders agreed that both large-scale nuclear and small modular 
reactors (“SMRs”) should be included as possible options for the model to select.  
• Stakeholders were divided over offshore wind build limits. Stakeholders had the option to 
either maintain a build limit of 3,400 megawatts (“MW”), corresponding to the Company’s 
existing lease areas, or raise the build limit to 6,000 MW, requiring the Company to procure a 
new 2,600 MW offshore wind development. Ultimately, stakeholders were split 50/50. Since 
stakeholder preferences were tied, the Company decided to utilize a build limit of 6,000 MW. 
The choice to increase the build limit is consistent with what stakeholders selected for other 
similar renewable resource build limits. 
• Stakeholders also strongly expressed the preference to model more battery technology. 48% 
of stakeholders voted to double the Company’s preferred build limits for storage. 38% of 
stakeholders selected the “other” option, and requested the Stakeholder Input Case model

==== 2026-integrated-resource-plan-update.pdf — page 117 ====
7 
 
go even further by tripling or having no build limits on storage at all. Only 14% of 
stakeholders requested to align with the Company’s preferred storage build limit. 
 
Analysis of the Stakeholder Input Case 
 
Figure 4: Stakeholder Input Case Modeling Results 
 
 
When put into the PLEXOS model, the Stakeholder Input Case is a notable outlier compared to the 
other portfolios submitted by the Company in the 2026 IRP. The Company recognizes this case is 
not the preference of one single stakeholder, but a combination of the inputs and preferences of 
multiple stakeholders representing a broad range of perspectives. 
The 2026 Stakeholder Input Case, however, is not a reasonable approach to resource planning for 
the following reasons:  
• Increasing build limits for solar, storage, and SMRs to infeasible amounts may have 
unintended consequences of making projects more difficult to site, such as by prompting 
additional land use restrictions and potential bans at the local level.  
• Like the Forced Retirements by 2045 Portfolio, the Stakeholder Input Case assumes 
appropriate location(s) would be available within the Commonwealth to build new large-scale 
nuclear units.  
• The incremental cost of the additional very large projects envisioned within the planning 
window of the stakeholder input case makes this case financially uncompetitive with the 
Company Preferred plan from an affordability perspective.

==== 2026-integrated-resource-plan-update.pdf — page 118 ====
8 
 
• When run through the short-term version of the PLEXOS model, the Stakeholder Input Case 
experienced occurrences of unserved energy, including during the summer peak months 
(Jun-Aug), indicating that this plan may not ensure reliable service to our customers. 
 
The Company appreciates the engagement and feedback provided by stakeholders during the 
stakeholder process.  
   
Looking to 2027 
The Company recognizes a number of new changes are coming to the IRP Stakeholder 
Engagement Process in 2027, as a result of legislation passed in the 2026 Virginia General 
Assembly Session.3 In the 2027 Stakeholder Engagement Process, the Company will be required to 
utilize a third-party facilitator selected by the SCC. Also, certain stakeholders will receive licenses to 
our modeling software, PLEXOS, and will be granted access to modeling inputs and assumptions as 
required by law. Due to these changes, the 2027 Stakeholder Engagement Process will likely be 
structured differently than prior years, including an earlier timeline for stakeholder engagement. 
Nevertheless, the Company will work with the SCC-selected facilitator to foster an engaging and 
meaningful process for all stakeholders to provide their feedback.  
 
Thank You to Participants 
The Company is grateful to each stakeholder for taking the time to engage throughout the 2026 
Stakeholder Engagement Process. We appreciate your thoughtful feedback, meaningful questions, 
and robust engagement, and we look forward to your continued participation in the next stakeholder 
process. The Company would also like to thank the Great Plains Institute for their facilitation 
services. 
 
Conclusion 
Dominion Energy’s 2026 Stakeholder Engagement Process successfully engaged a broad array of 
stakeholders, representing multiple interests and customer classes. Through a structured process 
designed to be accessible for stakeholders with a range of knowledge, the Company received 
meaningful feedback and provided ample opportunities for stakeholders to ask questions.  
Additionally, the Company retained the expertise of a neutral, third-party facilitator to further refine 
our engagement process. While the 2026 IRP is not subject to a formal evidentiary proceeding 
before the SCC, the Company provided multiple avenues for stakeholder feedback, including 
participation during meetings, the Stakeholder Input Case Survey, access to Company subject-
matter experts, as well as a dedicated website to receive questions and comments throughout the 
process.   
This process has continued to evolve as we seek feedback and build on the lessons of previous 
stakeholder processes and adapt to new requirements as needed. The IRP Stakeholder 
Engagement Process is iterative and constantly evolving. The Company remains committed to 
maintaining an open process to make improvements in future IRP cycles. 
  
 
3 House Bill 429 and Senate Bill 249 of the 2026 Acts of Assembly.

Background 
To support stakeholder engagement for its 2026 Integrated Resource Plan (“IRP”), Dominion 
Energy hired Great Plains Institute as a neutral, third-party convener with experience and 
expertise in similar engagement efforts. From February to October 2026, Great Plains Institute 
(““GPI”“) organized and facilitated a series of stakeholder engagement meetings on behalf of 
Dominion Energy (the “Company”) to inform the development of this engagement. As a third-
party neutral facilitator, GPI sought to ensure stakeholder perspectives and feedback relevant to 
the 2026 IRP could be shared and considered by the Company in a respectful, transparent 
format.  
Avenues for participant feedback included two stakeholder surveys, several online polling 
activities, and seven meetings with varying levels of technical detail held in both hybrid and 
virtual-only formats. GPI and Dominion Energy plan to hold one additional public stakeholder 
meeting in a webinar format on October 21, 2026, wherein the Company will share a high-level 
overview of the filed plan. 
The following document serves as a summary of the 2026 stakeholder engagement process, 
including parties engaged, meeting topics, and participant feedback. 
Stakeholder Identification 
For the 2026 IRP Stakeholder Engagement Process, GPI conducted outreach on behalf of 
Dominion Energy to the Company’s 2025 stakeholder list, which included participants from past 
IRP proceedings; staff from the Virginia State Corporation Commission (“SCC”) and North 
Carolina Utilities Commission (“NCUC”); other local, state, and federal officials; tribal nations; 
nonprofit groups; the military and defense sector; labor unions; businesses and large energy 
users; and individual citizens, among others. Dominion Energy also published notices in 
newspapers to expand outreach into rural and underserved communities. 
GPI handl
ed all stakeholder communications and meeting logistics on behalf of the Company 
through a single email address (DEVIRP2026@gpisd.net). GPI continued adding stakeholders 
to the email list as new members requested to join. In total, GPI and Dominion Energy engaged 
approximately 110 individual stakeholders in virtual and in-person meetings. Representatives 
from the following 61 organizations attended at least one stakeholder meeting or submitted a 
response to at least one stakeholder survey:

Engagement Process 
GPI and Dominion Energy undertook an engagement plan that consisted of two stakeholder 
surveys, six substantive public meetings with opportunities for feedback and discussion, one 
kickoff webinar, and one post-filing webinar. 
To inform the plan, GPI conducted a scoping survey to gather input on what topics stakeholders 
were most interested in discussing and learning about during the 2026 engagement process. 
This feedback directly informed the topics and agenda items for six substantive meetings 
covering the scope of the IRP, which were divided into two categories based on the intended 
audience’s familiarity with energy modeling:  
2

==== 2026-integrated-resource-plan-update.pdf — page 121 ====
• Br
oad engagement meetings (Kickoff Webinar, IRP Conference 1, IRP Conference 2,
Survey Results Meeting, and IRP Post-Filing Meeting) were intended for an audience
with little to no expertise in energy modeling.
• Modeling meetings (Modeling Meetings 1, 2, and 3) were intended to focus on topics of
interest to stakeholders with a greater degree of expertise in IRP-related modeling.
A core objective of these meetings was to provide opportunities for stakeholders to ask 
questions and build understanding to inform their responses to Dominion Energy’s stakeholder 
input case survey, which directly informed the stakeholder input case in the Company’s filed IRP 
update.

Meeting Logistics 
All meetings in this engagement process were open to all participants who wished to attend. 
Two IRP Conferences were held in a hybrid format at the Thomas F. Farrell II building in 
3

==== 2026-integrated-resource-plan-update.pdf — page 122 ====
R
ichmond, VA; participants had the option to attend these meetings in person or to participate 
virtually via WebEx. All other meetings were hosted virtually via WebEx. 
Before each meeting, GPI sent an email to the full stakeholder list requesting RSVPs by 
responding to the email message. In-person and virtual meeting logistics were then distributed 
to interested attendees by email, with slides sent out to attendees the day before each meeting. 
To enable constructive discussion, GPI established the following ground rules for all meeting 
participants.  
1. Respect each other and the time: Respect differences of perspective and the time we
hav
e together.
2. Focus on today’s topics: Please respect the scope of today’s meeting. Pending or
recently enacted legislation and open regulatory dockets are outside the scope of
today’s
 meeting.
3. Project and customer specifics are out of scope: Specific projects, including
tr
ansmission, distribution, and generation projects, are outside the scope of the IRP and
today’s
 meeting. Customer specifics are also out of scope.
Each meeting included presentation material paired with time for Q&A and discussion. 
Depending on the content and format of each meeting, GPI used a combination of the WebEx 
chat feature, WebEx Q&A feature, and Mentimeter poll questions to solicit participant feedback. 
During discussion sections of meetings, participants were encouraged to use WebEx’s virtual 
“raise hand” feature so that a facilitator could unmute them to ask their questions aloud. 
Dominion Energy tracked participant questions throughout each meeting and posted answers to 
them on a public website at the following link: https://devirp.dominionenergy.com/stakeholder-
questions-and-answers. GPI monitored the email inbox DEVIRP2026@gpisd.net for meeting 
attendance and administrative questions.  
The following sections offer high level summaries of each meeting, including topics discussed, 
participant feedback, attendance, and key takeaways. More detailed summaries of each 
meeting, along with meeting recordings and slide decks, are available at 
https://devirp.dominionenergy.com/stakeholder-materials. 
Scoping Survey 
On March 18, 2026, GPI distributed an initial scoping survey to the stakeholder email list on 
behalf of Dominion Energy. Participants had two weeks to submit responses to this survey. GPI 
asked respondents to identify and rank topics of interest that they would like Dominion Energy 
to discuss during engagement meetings. GPI also asked respondents to identify desired 
outcomes and expectations for the engagement process. 
Aggregated participant feedback regarding topics of interest (Question 1 and Question 2) 
resulted in the following list of priority topics, ranked in order of greatest interest: 
1. Cost & affordability
2. Load growth, including data center growth
3. Clean energy resources, including but not limited to:
4

==== 2026-integrated-resource-plan-update.pdf — page 123 ====
a. E
nergy efficiency
b. Storage resources
c. Microgrids & VPPs
4. VCEA requirements
5. Transmission planning
6. Reliability
Participants also shared open-ended feedback regarding pros and cons of deploying specific 
resources. Participants expressed interest in an energy system that is reliable, affordable, and 
clean; shared suggestions for how Dominion Energy should address state and federal policies 
in modeling; and shared desired outcomes for the stakeholder engagement process. 
GPI and Dominion Energy used participant responses to these questions to guide development 
of meeting agendas and presentations from Dominion Energy subject matter experts throughout 
the course of the engagement process.

stakeholder survey are reflected in the Stakeholder Input Case scenario modeled in this filing 
and also included in the slide deck from the August 14 meeting.

Appendix 3A: Virginia Bill Analysis 
The Company calculated projected bills for each customer class under each Primary Portfolio using 
two methodologies: (1) based on requirements set by the Virginia State Corporation Commission 
(“SCC”) (“Directed Methodology”); and (2) using a forecasted system and class sales growth and the 
associated class allocation factors (“Company Methodology”). The Directed Methodology requires 
the Company use constant class allocation factors across time and no sales growth, either at the 
system or class level, in its calculations. As discussed in prior IRP proceedings, the Company 
believes that this methodology overstates bill projections for the residential customer class because 
it does not reflect anticipated growth in sales, which is not expected to be uniform between classes, 
and shifts cost allocation as a result. 
It is not a plausible assumption that class allocation factors will remain constant or that there will be 
no sales growth. Changes in sales growth naturally alter the proportion of sales to each class and, 
thus, the costs allocated to each class. Notably, the proportion of costs allocated to the residential 
class is projected to decrease over time because of growth of energy sales to other customer 
classes. The past five years demonstrate not only that sales growth will continue but also that it will 
be different amongst classes.   
Given these concerns with the Directed Methodology, the Company has also calculated projected 
bills under each primary Portfolio using forecasted system and class sales growth and the 
associated class allocation factors. This methodology is referred to as the Company Methodology.

Appendix 4A: Load Forecast Methodologies 
 
The DOM Zone’s peak demand is growing faster than all other PJM zones 
Dominion Energy’s peak loads have been increasing each year, and the peak loads are expected to 
continue to grow. The DOM Zone is forecasted to grow faster than any other PJM zone. While growth in 
DSM and distributed solar offset the increases in summer peak demand associated with economic 
expansion, the increase in demand associated with data centers and EVs far exceeds these DSM and 
distributed solar offsets. 
Figure 4A-1: PJM DOM Zone Winter and Summer Peak Demand Forecast shows the PJM DOM Zone 
forecasted non-coincident peaks in winter and summer. Over the 20-year forecast horizon, winter and 
summer peaks are projected to grow by 3.9% and 4.1%, respectively, on a compound annual basis. 
Forecasted peaks assume normal weather, meaning that extreme weather events could cause actual peaks 
to greatly exceed the forecast in any given year and for sustained periods. The Company must plan its 
generation to meet customers’ needs in extreme weather events, not just normal weather.   
 
Figure 4A-1: PJM DOM Zone Winter and Summer Peak Demand Forecast

PJM Derived Load Forecast for DOM LSE  
 
The Company utilized the PJM DOM Zone Load Forecast as published in the 2026 PJM Load Forecast 
Report, dated January 14, 2026, in the development of the 2026 IRP Portfolios. PJM annually solicits 
information from its member electric distribution companies (“EDC”) and/or Load Serving Entities (“LSE”) 
regarding significant future block load increases, including data centers, that are known to the EDCs. The 
Company provided PJM the data center load forecast for its customers located in the DOM LSE including 
the retail choice customers (“Choice customers”). PJM then independently analyzed this and other LSE 
submissions, incorporated the information into its annual forecast at its discretion, developed a load forecast 
for all load zones within the PJM footprint, and published its report on the PJM website (the “PJM Dom Zone 
Load Forecast”). The DOM Zone is one of these load zones. 
As in prior IRPs, in order to properly use the PJM DOM Zone Load Forecast for modeling purposes, 
Dominion Energy converted that forecast to the DOM LSE level. This conversion is necessary for modeling 
purposes because it provides the Company’s customers’ demand (i.e., those customers the Company is 
obligated to serve). The PJM DOM Zone Load Forecast, in contrast, provides the demand for the entire 
DOM Zone, which includes customers served by other LSEs. The Company refers to this load forecast as 
the 2026 PJM Derived Load Forecast. 
To prepare the PJM Derived Load Forecast for the DOM LSE, the Company used the following process as 
diagrammed in Figure 4A-2 below. 
 Figure 4A-2: PJM DOM Zone Load Forecast conversion to DOM LSE Forecast flow chart 
 
  
The Company first scaled down the PJM DOM Zone peak load and energy forecasts to the DOM LSE level. 
The Company completed this in two parts. First, the Company adjusted the forecast by taking out PJM’s 
DOM Zone data center forecast and then applied a normalized historical DOM LSE-to-DOM Zone load ratio. 
The Company calculated the ratio by using a two-year average (2024 and 2025) of DOM LSE-to-DOM Zone 
annual energy, excluding data centers. This method of scaling down the PJM forecast ensures that the DOM 
LSE-to-DOM Zone ratio appropriately changes in the forecast period. 
Second, the Company then added back the DOM LSE portion of the data center forecast and removed the 
Choice forecast. Note that the data center forecast the Company incorporated into the PJM Derived Load

==== 2026-integrated-resource-plan-update.pdf — page 228 ====
3 
 
Forecast is produced by PJM, includes only the DOM LSE data center forecast, and does not include the 
forecast from NOVEC or other cooperatives in the DOM Zone. Finally, the Company removed all additional 
DSM savings incremental to 2025 (“incremental DSM”) to result in the PJM Derived Load Forecast used for 
the 2026 IRP.  
Overall, the 2026 PJM Derived Load Forecast anticipates a 2.8% and 3.8% CAGR for the DOM LSE 
summer non-coincident peak (“NCP”) demand and annual energy, respectively, over the Planning Period 
(2026-2046). Over the same period, the 2026 Company Load Forecast predicts a 2.5% and 3.4% CAGR for 
the DOM LSE summer non-coincident peak demand and annual energy, respectively. Forecasts for both 
energy (megawatt-hour (“MWh”)) and peaks (“MW”) are presented. As shown in Figure 4A-3 below, the 
2026 PJM Derived Load Forecast coincident peak is generally similar to the 2025 PJM Derived Load 
Forecast, particularly in the near and medium term. Figure 4A-4 also shows that the 2026 PJM Derived 
Load Forecast for energy is slightly higher than the 2025 PJM Derived Load Forecast in the near-to-medium 
term, diverging further in the out-years of the forecast.  
Figure 4A-3: 2026 vs 2025 PJM Derived Load Forecast - Coincident Peak

==== 2026-integrated-resource-plan-update.pdf — page 229 ====
4 
 
Figure 4A-4: 2026 vs 2025 PJM Derived Load Forecast – Energy2 
 
As described in Figure 4A-2, the transition from the DOM Zone forecast to the DOM LSE forecast includes 
a reduction for net incremental DSM. However, the effects of DSM and broader energy efficiency initiatives 
may already be reflected in the DOM Zone forecast through the historical load data used in PJM’s forecast 
development. Over the past several years, increasing adoption of energy-efficient technologies and 
programs has contributed to lower load growth, and these impacts are inherently represented within 
historical trends. Accordingly, the incremental DSM adjustment may partially overlap with efficiency-related 
effects already embedded in the PJM forecast, contributing to a potential downward bias in the DOM LSE 
forecast. The Company will continue to evaluate opportunities to refine its forecasting methodology and 
assumptions to appropriately account for these effects and mitigate the potential for forecast bias. 
 
 
Company Load Forecast 
The 2026 IRP also includes the Company’s internally developed peak demand and energy forecast for the 
DOM LSE (i.e., the Company Load Forecast). The Company Load Forecast includes forecasts of sales and 
associated drivers at the customer-class level, which results in a forecast that is better able to capture 
region-specific load characteristics.   
As an example, PJM’s forecast incorporates DSM reductions but does not specifically incorporate Company 
DSM programs or future savings targets. While the Company attempts to account for future DSM savings 
targets when calculating the PJM Derived Load Forecast, it must do so without any regard for DSM already 
embedded in PJM’s original DOM Zone forecast. As another example, although the Company has 
conducted a study to forecast EVs that is specific to its service territory, PJM has not been able to conduct 
such a detailed study for each LSE in its load zones. Additionally, the Company is able to adjust its internal 
load forecast to account for the impact of the incremental adoption of rooftop solar. Furthermore, converting 
 
2 Expressed in gigawatt hours (“GWh”).

==== 2026-integrated-resource-plan-update.pdf — page 230 ====
5 
 
the forecast from DOM Zone to DOM LSE entails complexities that are avoided by directly modeling the 
Company Load Forecast. 
 
At a high level, the Company Load Forecast is prepared using Company sales data and DOM LSE peak and 
energy data. Separate sales models are created for residential, commercial, industrial, government, and 
other municipal customers. Data centers are forecasted separately from other commercial customers given 
the scope and distinctive nature of the industry (see Data center load in the DOM Zone and DOM LSE 
below). The resulting sales forecast is then converted into an energy forecast using an estimated loss factor. 
This is followed by post-processing forecast adjustments for data centers, retail choice sales, DSM, 
distributed solar, and EVs. Finally, the peak forecast is derived from a detailed hourly model using historical 
weather simulation. Figure 4A-5 below presents the 2026 Company Load Forecast NCP and annual 
energy.

through the forecast horizon.

Retail Choice Adjustment to DOM LSE Load Forecast  
The load forecasts in this 2026 IRP include a downward adjustment for Choice Customers. To develop this 
forecast the Company first identified the group of current Choice Customers. The Company then determined 
the annual energy use for this set of customers over 2025. Finally, the Company shaped the total energy 
use into hourly intervals using historic Choice Customer interval data.

==== 2026-integrated-resource-plan-update.pdf — page 233 ====

The summation of each customer’s average annual energy and capacity use then formed the starting point 
for the Choice Customer forecast. Figure 4A-9 below identifies the Choice Customer peak demand and 
energy forecast adjustment in this 2026 IRP. The values in Figure 4A-9 represent non-data center 
customers only, as data center customers included in the forecast already exclude choice load.

Due to the uncertain nature of customer migration in or out of Choice, the Retail Choice Adjustment was 
held constant throughout the forecast period. Currently retail choice load is excluded from all IRP reference 
cases.       
 
Data Center Forecasting for the DOM LSE 
The Company has seen unprecedent levels of growth in both the size and number of requests for delivery 
points in the last several years, including the significant increase in volume and increased size from large-
load customers. As of February 2026, approximately 25,000 megawatts of large-load delivery point requests 
have been received with projected connection dates through December 31, 2031. Those requests continue 
to grow. Importantly, however, the 2025 forecast was not based on contracts. Dominion Energy uses a 
systematic process, refined over several years, to develop a data center billing demand forecast 
First, Dominion Energy identified the seven largest and/or fastest growing data center customers, creating 
seven customer specific segments. Next, it combined all other data center customers (approximately 47) 
into an eighth segment. The Company calculated an initial billing demand forecast for the eight customer 
segments by preparing three different demand forecasts (linear regression, polynomial regression, bass 
diffusion) for each customer segment resulting in 24 different demand models. Next, the Company applied 
customer intelligence (publicly available information, internal project communications with the customer, and 
industry reports, and customer provided forecasts) to select the appropriate demand model for each of the 
customer segments. If none of the three models aligned with customer intelligence as to future business 
growth, then an adjusted growth curve was used (e.g., a flat growth curve). The Company then used the 
historical monthly usage of demand to create the forecasted demand values by month within each year for 
each customer segment.  
Second, the Company used historical metered data to develop four different statistical models for the overall 
industry. These four models were averaged to develop the “low” forecast. Finally, the Company took an

==== 2026-integrated-resource-plan-update.pdf — page 234 ====
9 
 
average of the aggregate by-customer segment (“high”) and aggregate (“low”) forecasts to derive the 
“medium” scenario, which became the basis of the Company’s official submission to PJM. 
Third, the Company validated the forecast in two ways: (1) it compared the individual billing demand 
forecasts against customer provided forecasts, and (2) it compared the aggregate forecast to executed 
contracts-in-hand to determine the reasonableness of the forecast. 
Fourth, the Company prepared a MWh forecast by applying the historical average load factors to each of the 
selected customer segment models to derive a MWh forecast by segment, excluding retail choice MWhs. 
The aggregate of these individual MWh forecasts is used as the Company’s submission for sales. 
The fifth and final step in the process is to convert billing demand into coincident demand. The Company 
used the historical ratio of coincident demand to billing demand to determine the aggregate coincident 
demand for submission to PJM.  
 
The DOM LSE Data Center Contracting Process 
The Contracting Process for Data Centers3 
The connection process begins when a data center submits a request for service to Dominion Energy’s 
distribution team. The request must include a site plan or building layout, requested energization date, the 
capacity being requested including a ramp schedule, and meter voltage (primary or secondary voltage). 
The Company reviews this request and provides information to the customer, including a feasibility report to 
identify any critical flaws and high-level needs for energization. Upon receipt of this information, the 
customer decides whether to proceed to an Engineering Letter of Authorization (“ELOA”). 
Figure 4A-10 provides a brief overview of each step of a typical data center request process. These steps 
are also described in the subsequent narrative. 
 
3 https://sustainability.dominionenergy.com/GS-5%20Large%20Load%20Rate%20Class%20Report.pdf.

==== 2026-integrated-resource-plan-update.pdf — page 235 ====
10 
 
Figure 4A-10: Typical Data Center Request Process from Contact to Connection 
 
If the customer wishes to proceed, the first step in our contracting process is executing an ELOA. Execution 
of this agreement protects the Company, as discussed below, allows the distribution team to add the data 
center project to our queue, and begins the engineering study and design processes that are prerequisites 
to connect to the grid. At signing, a $250,000 deposit is required to support engineering and design work. If 
the project is complex or changes partway through the design process, resulting in costs exceeding 
$250,000, the Company issues an updated ELOA requiring an additional deposit for the estimated 
remaining costs. This protects the Company and its customers from incurring unnecessary design and 
engineering costs. 
After the project moves through the queue process and all engineering is completed, the customer is offered 
a Construction Letter of Agreement (“CLOA”). Here again, the customer must decide whether to proceed by 
signing the CLOA within 90 days of issuance. The CLOA contracts Dominion Energy to build infrastructure—
therefore, no significant capital investments are made until the customer executes this agreement. 
Importantly, the CLOA triggers three items, deposits for long lead time equipment, 100% reimbursement of 
all costs incurred if the project is canceled before energization, and the requirement to execute an Electric 
Service Agreement upon energization for the installed capacity. If a customer requests additional 
infrastructure beyond what is normally provided for new service connections, then that customer pays the 
incremental cost of that infrastructure via a facilities charge, as provided for in the Company’s approved 
Terms and Conditions. 
Dominion Energy then commences executing the project plan. Long-lead-time materials are ordered, a 
construction schedule is finalized, acquisition of third-party easements and permits begin, and onsite 
easements are provided to the customer or property owner for execution. 
The Company (or customer) will pursue substation permitting with the locality. In parallel, if required, the 
Company will file an application for a certificate of public convenience and necessity (“CPCN”) for the 
transmission line, including a recommended transmission line route and viable route alternatives with the 
SCC. As part of the CPCN proceeding, the SCC reviews and confirms the need for the new infrastructure 
and ultimately selects and approves the final route after notice and opportunity for hearing.

==== 2026-integrated-resource-plan-update.pdf — page 236 ====
11 
 
The final stage of contracting entails an Electric Service Agreement (“ESA”). Issued up to one year before 
energization—close to the end of construction—this document specifies all pertinent contractual provisions 
related to the provision of energy, including complying with the Company’s tariffs (discussed below) and 
terms and conditions. Collateral requirements, which were approved to become more stringent pursuant to a 
recent SCC ruling, are due to be paid before the customer’s meter is set and its project is energized.4

Dominion Energy 2Q Earnings Call).5

Additional Considerations for Data Center Load 
Data center customer load is unique. Data centers operate with a very high load factor, meaning the 
consumption of energy is very high relative to the level of demand. Said differently, data centers have a 
constant 24x7x365 energy profile. In addition to building infrastructure to serve these customers, the 
Company offers a number of DSM programs that data centers have and are able to take advantage of,

especially for customer-facing processes, far exceeds any economic value of participation under current 
incentive structures and market conditions.6

Appendix 4C: Demand-Side Management  
 
Dominion Energy offers energy conservation programs designed to assist our Virginia and North 
Carolina electric customers with saving energy and money. We advocate for cost -effective energy 
efficiency innovation in residences and businesses and develop demand-side management programs 
to support state and national policies focused on energy conservation and the goals around energy 
savings. The Company seeks to empower customers by providing them with the necessary information 
and solutions to manage their own energy use. Over the past 16 years, Dominion Energy’s programs 
have produced significant environmental benefits while providing customers with substantial energy 
savings that help lower monthly energy expenses. 
This appendix provides a description of the DSM planning process and an overview of active and 
rejected DSM program s. Additional information on the Company’s Demand- Side Management and 
Energy Efficiency programs in North Carolina can be found in their respective dockets.  
As noted in Section 4.2.1 of the 2026 IRP, from a modeling perspective the Company accounted for 
savings from its active DSM programs along with forecasted growth to those programs as a downward 
adjustment to the load forecast. There are several drivers that affect the Company’s ability to achieve 
energy and demand savings from DSM , including the cost-effectiveness of programs and measures 
and customers’ willingness to participate in active DSM programs. 
To develop the energy and capacity reductions used in the primary Portfolios, the Company used the 
energy efficiency savings targets established in Case No. PUR -2023-00227 for 2026- 2028 and 
continued these targets throughout the remaining 20-year planning horizon.  
For 2026, the Company used the savings it expects to achieve from its active DSM programs without 
any adjustment. This is because all programs capable of delivering savings in 2026 must have already 
been approved by the SCC in order to operate during that year. The SCC’s most recent approval  of 
DSM Programs, issued on August 3, 2026, was in Case No. PUR-2025-00210. All new programs and 
measures approved therein will be available to customers at the beginning of 2027  and have been 
included in the forecasted savings in this 2026 IRP. Any future DSM programs or measures capable 
of delivering incremental savings would not be available until 2028 at the earliest, pending regulatory 
approval. 
The Company’s 2026 IRP DSM adjustment is ambitious, with forecasted incremental energy savings 
growing from 802 GWh in 2026, to 2,725 GWh by 2031, and to 3,496 GWh by 2046.

==== 2026-integrated-resource-plan-update.pdf — page 255 ====
2 
 
Figure 1 
 
All savings are calculated on a net basis, meaning savings from “free riders”—customers participating 
and receiving an incentive through a utility-sponsored DSM program, but who would have taken the 
action to achieve savings even absent the incentive—are removed from the calculation. Said another 
way, only savings from customers actually incented by the DSM program to make an efficient change 
are counted.   
Achieving the forecasted level of energy savings will require diligence and cooperation among the 
Company and the many stakeholders who participate in the on- going DSM specific stakeholder 
process established by the Grid Transformation and Security Act of 2018 (“GTSA”). The remainder of 
this appendix will discuss the DSM planning process and stakeholder group, the DSM long-term plan, 
and additional specific analysis required by the GTSA. 
 
I.  DSM Planning Process  
 
The Company has historically used the following process related to its DSM programs: 
 
The GTSA established an independent moderator -led DSM stakeholder group, which helps to 
generate new program ideas. That stakeholder group meets a minimum of two times a year as a large 
group, with additional more frequent meetings by subgroups dedicated to specific topics of interest 
such as low-income specific programming or Evaluation, Measurement, and Verification (“EM&V”).

==== 2026-integrated-resource-plan-update.pdf — page 256 ====
3 
 
The Company takes stakeholder generated ideas and develops them into more concrete program 
parameters, which are then compiled into an RFP of candidate program designs and implementation 
services, which is sent annually  to qualified vendors. The Company develops assumptions for new 
DSM programs by engaging vendors through a competitive RFP process to submit proposals for 
candidate program design and implementation services. As part of the bid process, basic program 
design parameters and descriptions of candidate programs are requested. To the extent practical, the 
Company prefers that the program design vendor is the same vendor that implements the final 
implementation. The Company believes this enables as much continuity as possible from design to 
implementation.   
Once proposals through an RFP process are received, the Company’s energy conservation group 
works with the Company’s supply chain group to systematically review the proposals. Program designs 
are reviewed for responsiveness to the RFP, practicality of the design, technology requirements, 
staffing plan, marketing plan, reasonableness of the measures proposed, overlap with existing 
measures, cost reasonableness, previous experience, work history with the Company, expected ability 
to deliver the services proposed, and ability of the proposing firm to comply with the Company’s terms 
and conditions, data protection requirements, and financial requirements. Proposals must contain 
detailed information regarding measure load profiles and market penetration projections in a specific 
format which allows modeling of the program as a demand- side resource when compared against 
other resources, including supply-side resources. 
Candidate designs that are judged to be reasonable, based on preliminary review, are evaluated for 
cost-effectiveness from a multi -perspective approach using four of the standard tests from the 
California Standard Practice Manual: (i) the Participant Test, (ii) Utility Cost Test, (iii) Total Resource 
Cost Test, and (iv) Ratepayer Impact Measure Test.  Each test uses the net present value (“NPV”) of 
costs and benefits. Tests are conducted at a program and portfolio level. 
The Company has developed the Load Management Tool to perform the cost/benefits test leveraging 
avoided cost benefits obtained from the Company’s most recent IRP . The Company reviews the 
results of all four of the NPV cost/benefit test scores to evaluate whether to file for regulatory approval 
of a particular potential program, extension, or modification.   
If the programs are cost -effective based on the modeling results, or otherwise legislatively stated to 
be in the public interest, the programs and pilots are filed with the SCC for approval. The SCC approval 
process lasts approximately eight months. For the programs that are active, the Company works with 
the RFP suppliers to finalize a contract for full implementation of the program. Once all details are 
finalized, a new DSM program  or pilot  can be launched for participation by eligible customers. 
Programs that meet the statutory criteria in Virginia are then, when feasible and practicable on a 
smaller scale for the targeted North Carolina customer segment, brought forth in the following year to 
the NCUC for consideration. 
Finally, the Company conducts EM&V of all active DSM programs and files the annual EM&V report 
with the SCC and NCUC in June of each year. Results are shown for the prior calendar year on specific 
metrics, including program participation, spend, energy, and demand savings. Based on stakeholder 
feedback, these EM&V filings also include a “dashboard” of metrics most of interest to stakeholders. 
Some highlights from 2025 include:

III.  Rejected DSM Programs 
 
A list of the rejected DSM programs from prior integrated resource planning cycles is shown in 
Appendix 4G. These are DSM programs that were not found to be cost-effective when modeled during 
a particular planning cycle. Rejected programs may be re- evaluated and included in future DSM 
portfolios. 
 
IV.  GTSA Energy Efficiency Analysis 
 
Enactment Clause 18 of the GTSA required, “That as part of its integrated resource plans filed between 
2019 and 2028, any Phase II Utility, as that term is defined in subdivision A 1 of § 56- 585.1 of the 
Code of Virginia, shall incorporate into its long-term plan for energy efficiency measures policy goals 
of reduction in customer bills, particularly for low -income, elderly, veterans, and disabled customers; 
reduction in emissions; and reduction in the utility's carbon intensity.” 
In its 2021 DSM filing, Case No. PUR -2021-00247, the Company filed a long- term plan for the 
Company’s DSM initiatives with the goal of setting forth an achievable strategy for meeting the Virginia 
Clean Economy Act (“VCEA”) energy efficiency targets, as well as the state energy and policy goals 
noted above. The long-term plan provides a vision and pathways for making every practicable effort 
to achieve the legislative goals over short-, medium-, and long-term time frames.  The long-erm plan 
addresses: (i) strategic vision; (ii) achievability of GTSA and VCEA energy efficiency goals; (iii) risks, 
challenges, and opportunities stemming from legislative and regulatory changes; (iv) sector profiles, 
program design recommendations, and implementation pathways aligned with goals and high- level 
timelines; (v) approaches for adapting to an evolving customer market and advancements in 
technology; and (vi) high level forecast of energy and demand impacts, program costs, and cost -
effectiveness. 
The Company immediately began addressing the recommendations contained within the long- term 
plan and has made proposals to the SCC consistent with the recommendations therein as part of its 
filings for DSM in 2021 -2024. The Company has made considerable progress since the 
implementation of a  portfolio marketing strategy aimed at increasing overall awareness of its DSM 
programs and benefits of adopting energy conservation technologies and behaviors.

savings targets for the 2026-2028 period established in Case No. PUR-2023-00227.

goals, reduce the number of RECs required for RPS compliance, and benefit participating customers 
through lower energy usage and resulting bills. The Company will continue to actively participate in 
the stakeholder forum, which provides transparency and inclusivity in the DSM planning process as 
part of its efforts to achieve the DSM policy goals set by the Commonwealth. 
Enactment Clause 18 of the GTSA also directed that utility considerations of energy efficiency within 
its long-term plan shall include analysis of the following:  
• Energy efficiency programs for low -income customers in alignment with billing and credit 
practices; 
• Energy efficiency programs that reflect policies and regulations related to customers with 
serious medical conditions; 
• Programs specifically focused on low -income customers, occupants of multifamily housing,

• Options for combining distributed generation, energy storage, and energy efficiency for 
residential and small business customers;  
• The extent that electricity rates account for the amount of customer electricity bills in the 
Commonwealth and how such extent in the Commonwealth compares with such extent in 
other states, including a comparison of the average retail electricity price per kWh by rate class 
among all 50 states; 
• An analysis of each state’ s primary fuel sources for electricity generation, accounting for

• Other issues as appropriate.

The Company’s Residential Income and Age Qualifying Home Improvement Bundle Program provides 
in-home energy assessments and installation of select energy -saving products at no cost to eligible 
participants. Additionally, the Company offers certain EnergySTAR measures such as EnergySTAR 
appliances, EnergySTAR ceiling fans, and EnergySTAR windows to low-income customers.

program offerings did not expire and to promote greater operational efficiencies with the

performing the program field work and installing select energy -saving program measures.  The 
program is available to qualified customers in the Company’s Virginia service territory who earn 60%

available to customers who are 60 years or older with a household income of 120% or less of the state

multifamily homes, and mobile homes.

The Company has and continue s to work with the Department of Housing and Community 
Development to establish alignment with programs where helpful and beneficial.   
 
Electricity Rate and Consumption Comparison 
Electricity bills are driven by a combination of electricity rates and electricity consumption. The 
following charts show where each state and the Company falls by electricity rate and consumption. 
In the residential sector, the Company and Virginia as a whole fall within a cluster of mostly southern 
states with below -average rates and relatively high consumption. The consumption level reflects a 
high saturation of electric heating equipment compared to other parts of the U.S., paired with high 
cooling loads.

In the commercial sector, Virginia is an extreme outlier in consumption per customer, averaging more 
than 130,000 kWh per year. The Company is one of three utilities in Virginia with average commercial 
consumption over 100,000 kWh per year; the others are the City of Harrisonburg, Appalachian Power 
Co., and Virginia Tech Electrical Services. In contrast, the utility with the lowest average commercial 
consumption is Northern Neck Elec Coop, Inc with less than 16,000 kWh per commercial customer.    
The primary drivers of commercial consumption are the size of the customer (i.e., building square feet, 
number of employees) and the type of building activity. Denser urban areas tend to have larger 
commercial buildings and therefore higher average commercial consumption, and the Company’s 
service territory captures many of Virginia’s  densest urban areas. The Company also has a high 
concentration of data centers among its commercial customers. Data centers are extremely energy 
intensive, as the densely packed computing equipment they contain produces waste heat that drives 
high space cooling loads. Because of the extreme differences among commercial customers, building 
efficiencies are typically compared based on energy intensity ( i.e., energy use per square foot) and

The Company’s Long-Term Plan (“LTP”) 2.0, which was part of the 2025 DSM p roceeding, provides 
a detailed overview of the Company’s progress and continued commitment to improvement , which 
includes optimizing customers’ participation in the Company’s DSM Program portfolio offering and 
experience in future DSM programs. The LTP 2.0 outlines that energy savings targets for years 2026-
2028 cannot be achieved in a cost-effective manner. The Company’s third-party consultant conducted 
a scenario analysis, based on measure- level inputs from the Company’s 2024 Potential Study, to 
explore pathways towards meeting the targets set forth in Case No. PUR -2023-00227, resulting in 
Scenarios 1 and 2.  The initial pathway, Scenario 1, maximizes the achievable amount of cost-effective 
energy savings and found that savings would fall short of set target. Scenario 2’s pathway c ould 
theoretically achieve the Commission ordered goals for 2026- 2028, however, it is not cost-effective. 
Specifically, Scenario 2 would require an additional and imprudent investment of more than $1.4 billion 
over the three- year period. The Company is continuing to evaluate the  best options set forth for 
Scenario 1 and is also pursuing another potential study that is anticipated to be complete at the end 
of 2026.

Non-Residential New Construction Program  
Target Class:  Non-Residential  
VA Program Type: Energy Efficiency  
NC Program Type: Energy Efficiency 
VA Duration:  2024 – 2046 
NC Duration:  Future 
 
Program Description: 
This Program provides qualifying non-residential customers with incentives to install energy 
efficient measures in their new construction project. Program engineers will determine what 
potential energy efficiency upgrades are of interest to the owner and feasible within their 
budget. These measures coupled with basic facility design data will be analyzed to determine 
the optimized building design. This in-depth analysis will be performed using building energy 
simulation models, which will allow for “bundles” of measures to be tested for potential energy 
savings gains from interactive effects. The results will be presented to the facility owner to 
determine which measures(s) are to be installed. The proposed program design targets three 
main building-type categories –commercial buildings, industrial buildings, and data centers.

This Program provides an incentive to residential customers to purchase a qualifying smart 
thermostat through the Company’s online marketplace platform and brick and mortar 
participating retailers. The Program is open to several thermostat manufacturers, makes, and 
models that meet or exceed the Energy Star requirements and have communicating 
technology. Rebates for the purchase of a smart thermostat are provided on a one-time 
basis. 
 
Program Marketing: 
The Company uses a number of marketing activities to promote its approved DSM programs, 
including but not limited to: direct mail, bill inserts, web content, social media, and outreach 
events.   
 
Residential Smart Thermostat Demand Response Program 
Target Class:  Residential  
VA Program Type: Demand Response 
NC Program Type: Demand Response 
VA Duration:  2026 – 2046 
NC Duration:  Future 
 
Program Description: 
The Residential Smart Thermostat (DR) Program is a peak demand response program 
through which demand response is called by the Company during times of peak system 
demand throughout the year and thermostats of participating customers would be adjusted to 
achieve a specified amount of load reduction while maintaining reasonable customer comfort 
through a gradual increase in home temperature and allowing customers to opt-out of specific 
events if they choose to do so. Customers receive one-time enrollment incentive and an 
annual incentive for participating in the program. 
 
Program Marketing: 
The Company uses a number of marketing activities to promote its approved DSM programs, 
including but not limited to: direct mail, bill inserts, web content, social media, and outreach 
events.   
 
Non-Residential Data Center Program  
Target Class:  Non-Residential

VA Program Type: Energy Efficiency  
NC Program Type: Energy Efficiency 
VA Duration:  2026 – 2046 
NC Duration:  Future 
 
Program Description: 
This Program provides qualifying non-residential customers with incentives to install energy 
efficiency measures related to equipment in and operation of data centers. Program services, 
as well as program measure installation, for this Program will be delivered through a network 
of qualified contractors and/or consultants with the appropriate specialization and experience 
to provide relevant, up-to-date advice on the measures included in the proposed program 
design. The new program design builds off the momentum of the existing DSM Phase X Data 
Center and Server Room Program while incorporating an expanded list of energy efficiency 
measures and funding for small, medium-sized, and larger data center customers. The 
program design measure list includes computer and power distribution equipment, HVAC, 
lighting, controls, and whole-building analysis options.   
 
Program Marketing:

including but not limited to: direct mail, bill inserts, web content, social media, and outreach 
events. Because this program is implemented using a program implementation vendor and/or 
contractor network, customers will enroll in the program by contacting a participating 
contractor. The Company utilizes the contractor network to market the programs to 
customers as well.

Non-Residential Distributed Generation Program (DR) 
Target Class:  Non-Residential 
VA Program Type: Demand-Side Management 
VA Duration:  2026 – 2046  
 
Program Description:  
The Program provides qualifying customers with an incentive to curtail load by operating 
backup generation upon request. The Program is implemented by a contractor who is 
responsible for enabling remote operation and monitoring the customer’s power generators, 
and for dispatching load during curtailment events under the direction of the Company. The 
program will provide participating customers a monthly incentive to allow their on-site backup 
generators to be remotely activated by the program implementation vendor during load 
curtailment events.   
 
Program Marketing: 
Marketing is handled by the Company’s implementation vendor. 
 
Non-Residential Curtailment Demand Response (DR) 
Target Class:  Non-Residential  
VA Program Type: Demand Response  
VA Duration:  2026 – 2046

==== 2026-integrated-resource-plan-update.pdf — page 280 ====
17 
 
Program Description:  
The program design targets medium sized and large commercial and industrial customers to 
curtail their energy usage using manual load curtailment during times of peak system 
demand. Each participating customer (facility) will have a curtailment plan developed, also 
known as a load reduction plan, which is specific to the facility and guided by engineering 
assessments put together by the program implementation vendor in collaboration with facility 
staff, factoring in the opportunity cost of participation, facility equipment and operations, and 
staff availability.   
 
Program Marketing: 
Marketing is handled by the Company’s implementation vendor.

Appendix 4E: Description of Recently 
Approved DSM Programs  
 
Non-Residential Energy Services (EE) 
Target Class:  Non-Residential  
VA Program Type: Energy Efficiency  
NC Program Type: Energy Efficiency 
VA Duration:  Proposed  
NC Duration:   Future 
 
Program Description: 
The Program design is a comprehensive energy services program that integrates and expands upon the 
existing DSM IX Building Optimization, DSM IX Building Automation, and DSM IX Customer Engagement 
programs, streamlining the three programs and incorporating new program pathways and new program 
measures. The intent of the unified program approach is to provide commercial customers with additional 
energy savings opportunities in their daily targeted operations and maintenance related savings 
opportunities. 
 
Program Marketing: 
The Company uses a number of marketing activities to promote its approved DSM programs, including but 
not limited to: direct mail, bill inserts, web content, social media, and outreach events. Because this 
program is implemented using a contractor network, customers will enroll in the program by contacting a 
participating contractor. The Company utilizes the contractor network to market the programs to customers 
as well. 
 
Residential Home Energy Services (EE) 
Target Class:  Residential  
VA Program Type: Energy Efficiency  
NC Program Type: Energy Efficiency 
VA Duration:  Proposed  
NC Duration:   Future 
 
Program Description: 
This Program is a comprehensive and unified residential home energy evaluation program offering that 
consists of a no-cost introductory in-home energy audit, no cost virtual audit, no-cost welcome kits and an 
optional comprehensive BPI audit. The program will also be available for qualifying residential customers 
residing in manufactured housing and multi-family dwellings. The program consolidates five previous 
standalone program offerings (Welcome Kits, Virtual Audit, Retrofit, Multi-family, and Manufactured 
Housing) under one single program offering to provide customers greater flexibility and ease of finding 
energy savings solutions.

==== 2026-integrated-resource-plan-update.pdf — page 296 ====
2 
 
Program Marketing: 
The Company uses a number of marketing activities to promote its approved DSM programs, including but 
not limited to: direct mail, bill inserts, web content, social media, and outreach events. Because this 
program is implemented using a contractor network, customers will enroll in the program by contacting a 
participating contractor. The Company utilizes the contractor network to market the programs to customers 
as well.  
 
Non-Residential HVAC for Small and Medium Sized Business Customers (DR) (VPP) 
Target Class:  Non-Residential  
VA Program Type: Demand Response 
NC Program Type: Demand Response 
VA Duration:  Proposed  
NC Duration:   No 
 
Program Description: 
The Non-residential HVAC for Small and Medium Business (“SMB”) Demand Response (“DR”) Program is 
a peak demand response program through which DR events will be called by the Company during times of 
system peak. Thermostats of participating SMB customers will be adjusted to achieve a specified amount 
of load reduction while maintaining reasonable facility comfort through a gradual change in business 
temperature and allowing customers to opt out of specific events if they choose to do so. Any SMB facility 
with HVAC load controlled by a smart thermostat will be eligible to participate in the program.  
 
Program Marketing: 
The Company uses a number of marketing activities to promote its approved DSM programs, including but 
not limited to: direct mail, bill inserts, web content, social media, and outreach events. Because this 
program is implemented using a contractor network, customers will enroll in the program by contacting a 
participating contractor. The Company utilizes the contractor network to market the programs to customers 
as well. 
 
Residential Electric Vehicle Managed Charging DR Pilot (Non-TOU and TOU rate) (DR) (VPP) 
Target Class:  Residential  
VA Program Type: Demand Response 
NC Program Type: Demand Response 
VA Duration:  Proposed  
NC Duration:  No 
 
Program Description: 
The proposed pilot design offers qualifying residential customers, both those on time-of-use (“TOU”) and 
non-TOU rate schedules who have an electric vehicle with the year-round opportunity to participate in a 
managed charging strategy during off-peak periods while ensuring vehicles are charged with lower-cost 
energy during selected times. The pilots will also be available to be called upon by the Company during 
peak system demand.

Program Marketing: 
The Company uses a number of marketing activities to promote its approved DSM programs, including but 
not limited to: direct mail, bill inserts, web content, social media, and outreach events.   
 
Residential Income and Age Qualifying (IAQ) Battery Storage Purchase Pilot  
Target Class:  Non-Residential  
VA Program Type: Energy Efficiency 
NC Program Type: Energy Efficiency 
VA Duration:  Proposed  
NC Duration:   No 
 
Program Description: 
The proposed pilot will provide income and age qualifying (“IAQ”) residential customers with a no cost 
battery energy storage system installation by a qualified battery storage installer. The pilot will target IAQ 
customers who have previously participated in the Company’s DSM Phase IX House Bill 2789 Solar Pilot, 
who had photovoltaic solar panels installed at their residence.  
 
Program Marketing: 
The Company uses a number of marketing activities to promote its approved DSM programs, including but 
not limited to: contractor network, weatherization service provider network, direct mail, bill inserts, web 
content, social media, and outreach events. 
 
Residential Income and Age Qualifying (IAQ) Battery Storage Pilot Demand Response (DR) (VPP) 
Target Class:  Non-Residential  
VA Program Type: Demand Response 
NC Program Type: Demand Response 
VA Duration:  Proposed  
NC Duration:   No 
 
Program Description: 
The proposed IAQ DR pilot will require IAQ customers who receive a no-cost battery energy storage 
system through the IAQ Battery Purchase Pilot to participate in the DR program and discharge their home 
battery storage system when called upon during peak electrical demand, along with other times that may 
provide services to the grid.  
 
Program Marketing: 
The Company uses a number of marketing activities to promote its approved DSM programs, including but 
not limited to: contractor network, weatherization service provider network, direct mail, bill inserts, web 
content, social media, and outreach events.   
 
Residential Battery Storage Pilot Demand Response (DR) (VPP) 
Target Class:  Non-Residential  
VA Program Type: Demand Response 
NC Program Type: Demand Response

NC Duration:   No 
 
Program Description: 
The four-year pilot will provide an incentive for residential customers to discharge their home battery 
storage system when called upon during peak electrical demand, along with other times that may provide 
grid services to the grid.  
 
Program Marketing: 
The Company uses a number of marketing activities to promote its approved DSM programs, including but 
not limited to: program implementation vendor, direct mail, bill inserts, web content, social media, and 
outreach events.   
 
Bring Your Own Device (BYOD) Aggregator Access Pilot (DR) (VPP) 
Target Class:  Non-Residential  
VA Program Type: Demand Response 
NC Program Type: Demand Response 
VA Duration:  Proposed  
NC Duration:   No 
 
Program Description: 
The BYOD Aggregator Access Pilot provides qualified aggregators the opportunity to enroll residential, 
commercial and industrial customers with eligible DER technologies, which will include EV chargers, smart 
thermostats, and water heaters across the Company’s diverse customer segments. 
 
Program Marketing: 
The Company uses a number of marketing activities to promote its approved DSM programs, including but 
not limited to: program implementation vendor, direct mail, bill inserts, web content, social media, and 
outreach events.

Appendix 4I: Cost Assumptions 
 
Commodity Price Assumptions 
 
The Company utilizes a single source—ICF—to provide multiple scenarios for the commodity price forecasts to 
ensure consistency in methodologies and assumptions. The key assumptions on market structure and the use of an 
integrated, internally consistent fundamentals-based modeling methodology remain consistent with those utilized by 
ICF in prior years’ commodity forecasts. 
 
Capacity Price Forecasting Methodology 
 
In most wholesale electricity markets, electric power generators are paid for providing: 
• Energy: the actual electricity consumed by customers; 
• Capacity: standing ready to provide a specified amount of electric energy; and, 
• Ancillary services: a variety of operations needed to maintain grid stability and security, including 
frequency control, spinning reserves, and operating reserves. 
 
The purpose of a mandatory capacity market is to encourage new investments where they are most needed on the 
grid.  PJM Interconnection, LLC’s (“PJM”) capacity market, the Reliability Pricing Model (i.e., the RPM), ensures 
long-term grid reliability by procuring the appropriate amount of supply- and demand-side resources needed to meet 
predicted peak demand in the future.  In a capacity market, utilities or other electricity suppliers are required to 
purchase adequate resources to meet their customers’ demand plus a reserve amount.  Suppliers offer supply- or 
demand-side resources into the capacity market at a price.  To the extent the supply offer clears the market, then 
those capacity resources are obligated to supply energy (or reduce energy in the case of demand-side resources) 
when dispatched or pay penalty fees. 
The RPM is designed to provide financial incentives to attract and maintain sufficient capacity to meet the load 
demands anticipated by PJM; in concept, revenues from energy and ancillary services plus capacity payments 
should equal the amount necessary to attract new entry.  Parallel to the actual market construct, forecasting of long-
term capacity prices is based on estimating the amount of capacity revenue a generation resource requires, in 
addition to revenue from energy and ancillary services.  The capacity revenue forecast represents the amount by 
which a resource’s cost exceeds its forecasted wholesale electricity market revenues.  The basic concept utilized in 
forecasting is that in order to maintain appropriate reserve levels to assure reliable electric service, generating 
resources will require sufficient revenue to cover expenses and, when necessary, support the required new 
investment.  When wholesale market energy and ancillary services revenue is not sufficient, then capacity revenues 
are required to fill this gap. 
When forecasting capacity prices over long periods, it is reasonable to assume markets will move toward equilibrium 
and will provide sufficient revenue to support existing resources and incent investment in new resources that require 
equity returns on the capital expended for development and construction of the new resource.  In markets with 
deficient capacity, new resources generally set the capacity price.  These resources require revenue to cover 
significant going forward capital expenditures and equity returns.  Because of this, the capacity price tends to be 
higher in markets with capacity deficiency.  However, over the long term, the market is expected to move to an

==== 2026-integrated-resource-plan-update.pdf — page 316 ====
2 
 
equilibrium status where sufficient revenues are provided, which assures adequate resource capacity and 
encourages market efficiency.  Note that while long-term forecasts tend toward an equilibrium pricing, it is expected 
that actual markets will continue to follow an up-and-down cycle that moves around equilibrium levels.  Long-term 
forecasts for capacity focus on the equilibrium level pricing rather than attempting to estimate the cyclical movement. 
 
Virginia REC Forecasting Methodology 
  
The Virginia Clean Economy Act (“VCEA”) instituted a mandatory renewable portfolio standard (“RPS”) Program in 
Virginia under which Dominion Energy must satisfy annual requirements for the sale of renewable energy.  
Beginning in 2027, 75% of the renewable energy certificates (“RECs”) used for the RPS Program compliance must 
come from resources located in Virginia, with additional requirements governing the type of facilities that qualify.  In 
addition, beginning with compliance each 2026, 4.5% of the required RECs must be generated by qualifying Virginia 
distributed energy resources with a nameplate capacity of 1 MW or less.  
The majority of Virginia RPS-eligible sources qualify for RPS compliance in multiple states.  A large and growing 
number of corporate buyers also procure and retire RECs to either sell in the market or meet their corporate-specific 
sustainability goals.  Therefore, the Company competes with corporate buyers for the purchase of qualifying RECs.  
The ability of other entities to bank eligible RECs in other jurisdictions further complicates REC availability analysis.  
We estimate that the Company’s need for RECs will grow from approximately 14 million in 2025 to approximately 46 
million in 2035.  These numbers incorporate adjustments of the REC forecast for a growing volume of accelerated 
clean energy buyer customers who meet their REC needs with contracts within PJM. If the REC market is 
undersupplied, the market price of RECs is likely to get close to the VCEA imposed deficiency payment.  
 
Commodity Price Scenarios 
In the 2026 IRP, the Company utilized six commodity scenarios: 
• Base Case with VA in RGGI (“Base Case”)  
• Sensitivity with VCEA Retirements included 
• Sensitivity with No VCEA Rules applicable 
• Sensitivity with No Data Center Load Growth in DOM Zone 
• Sensitivity with High Fuel Price 
• Sensitivity with Low Fuel Price 
 
As with all forecasts, there remain multiple possible outcomes for future prices that fall outside of the commodity 
prices developed for this 2026 IRP. History has shown that unforeseen events can result in significant changes in 
market fundamentals.  The effects of unforeseen events should be considered when evaluating the viability of long-
term planning objectives.  The commodity price forecasts analyzed in the 2026 IRP present reasonably likely 
outcomes given the current understanding of market fundamentals, but do not present all possible outcomes. 
 
Base Case Commodity Forecast 
The Base Case commodity forecast was developed for the Company to address a future market environment where 
impacts of recent supply chain and commodity price dislocations are incorporated into projections, natural gas 
continues to be a dominant marginal source of generation in PJM over the time horizon, tax credits available to
